Title: Machine Learning
Aided Design and Optimization of
Thermal Metamaterials
Text:

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has advanced material research
that
were previously intractable, for example, the machine learning (ML)
has been able to predict some unprecedented thermal properties. In
this review, we first elucidate the methodologies underpinning discriminative
and generative models, as well as the paradigm of optimization approaches.
Then, we present a series of case studies showcasing the application
of machine learning in thermal metamaterial design. Finally, we give
a brief discussion on the challenges and opportunities in this fast
developing field. In particular, this review provides: (1) Optimization
of thermal metamaterials using optimization algorithms to achieve
specific target properties. (2) Integration of discriminative models
with optimization algorithms to enhance computational efficiency.
(3) Generative models for the structural design and optimization of
thermal metamaterials.
Over the past few decades,
material research has witnessed remarkable
progress, addressing diverse challenges encompassing energy, manufacturing,
electronic information technology, and biochemical applications. Researchers
and engineers have paid considerable attentions to the identification
and fabrication of materials exhibiting optimal and unprecedented
functions and performance. However, due to the constraints imposed
by the chemical composition and internal bonds of natural materials,
further enhancements in their properties have been limited to a certain
extent. To overcome this limitation, an alternative approach has been
proposed: designing a new class of materials: metamaterials1,2 that possess extraordinary properties beyond those of natural materials.
These unique properties are a result of deliberately engineered structures.
The concept of metamaterials was initially proposed by Veselago
in the 1960s. He theoretically predicted the existence of materials
with negative permittivity and negative permeability, thus a negative
refractive index. Pendry et al.3−7 demonstrated the implementation of these materials by constructing
structures on a scale comparable to electromagnetic wavelengths. In
the early stage, metamaterials research predominantly focused on achieving
negative refractive indices, artificial magnetism, and superlens effects
within the microwave region. As the field progressed, investigations
have been expanded to the range of terahertz and optical frequencies.8 The remarkable advancements in metamaterials
have resulted in a plethora of impressive novel applications including
but not limited to cloaking,9−11 super lens,12 super thin antenna,13 perfect
light absorber or selective light emitter, and ultrahigh capacity
storage devices, etc.14−17 The success of electromagnetic metamaterials has inspired extensive
applications in other fields such as acoustics, mechanics, heat transfer,
and even hydrodynamics.18−21 The fascinating properties of metamaterials arise
from their artificial structures rather than their intrinsic composition.22−24 For instance, in electromagnetic metamaterials, the refractive index
can be tailored to values less than one through careful design of
the unit cell’s geometric parameters.25 Therefore, the geometry of the metamaterial’s unit cell plays
a pivotal role in achieving the desired properties.
How to figure
out the correspondence between structures and functions
is becoming an urgent and challenging task in materials research and
applications. Traditionally, like in Edison’s discovery of
tungsten as a filament for lamps, people heavily rely on human being’s
efforts of the trial-and-error. Usually, a proposed structure is designed
and fabricated and then is evaluated through simulations or experiments
until the desired targets are achieved. However, this approach’s
inherent nature renders it inefficient in addressing materials design
problems.26 Another approach involves employing
theoretical analysis to guide the design process. By establishing
physics-based models, researchers can gain a comprehensive understanding
of how different geometric and material parameters influence the final
properties, leading to the desired structure. Nevertheless, this method
demands profound knowledge and expertise to address specific research
questions and becomes challenging to widely applications, especially
as the design parameters increase rapidly. Both of the above design
methods rely heavily on human intelligence and necessitate the use
of efficient optimization algorithms that can operate automatically
to handle large space of design parameters effectively.
In recent
decades, researchers have employed two main categories
of optimization algorithms to address the inverse design problems
of metamaterials: (1) gradient-based algorithms, such as the level-set
method or adjoint method, and (2) gradient-free algorithms, which
encompass evolutionary approaches (e.g., genetic algorithm or particle
swarm optimization) and heuristic algorithms (e.g., simulated annealing
algorithm).27 Once appropriate hyperparameters
are set, both classes of methods can be operated automatically without
the need for human assistance or intervention.
Gradient-based
methods necessitate researchers to possess a profound
understanding of the derivatives of the cost function derived from
design parameters. However, these algorithms are prone to being trapped
in a local optimum, as their optimization results heavily depend on
the initial guess of the solution.28 In
contrast, gradient-free approaches exhibit the capability to converge
to a global optimum by stochastically exploring the design space.29 Their optimization performance is rarely affected
by the algorithm’s initialization. Notably, as numerous objective
functions in metamaterial design are nondifferentiable, gradient-free
methods offer distinct advantages without requiring gradient information.
Consequently, they are more accessible to a wider range of researchers.
Nevertheless, gradient-free approaches still rely on numerical simulations
to characterize the materials’ properties and performance,
verifying the design proposals and refining the searching strategy.
While these stochastic approaches have advantageous for many design
problems, they may become inadequate for more complex cases due to
their random-search nature, which can lead to significant time consumption
when optimizing devices with large degrees of freedom design spaces.30 Moreover, lacking gradient information to guide
the optimization direction often results in slower convergence to
a global optimum compared to gradient-based algorithms.
The
wealth of data generated by materials research has propelled
materials science toward data-driven questions.31−34 Advances in computing power and
increased storage capacity have facilitated the application of artificial
intelligence (AI) in designing metamaterials, leading to a significant
surge in interest and momentum.35,36 Machine learning (ML)
is a subset of AI that utilizes statistical techniques to empower
computer systems in making predictions for the future. This is achieved
by training the systems on available data and allowing them to learn
from their own experiences. Among various ML models, deep learning
(DL) has emerged as a particularly promising approach and has found
application in numerous scientific and engineering domains. Specifically,
deep neural network (DNN)-based architectures, comprising multiple
hidden layers, demonstrate a remarkable ability to learn and represent
complex functions, thus uncovering underlying relationships between
variables.37 DL has found applications
in the field of heat transfer, including predicting thermal conductivity
and thermal boundary resistance,38 studying
transport phenomena,39 modeling boiling
heat transfer,40 and solving thermal radiation
problems.41 Machine learning models can
be broadly classified into two types: discriminative and generative
networks. Discriminative networks excel in regression and classification
tasks.42 In regression tasks, the goal
is to reveal relationships within the training data, where input–output
mappings are represented as single-valued functions that support one-to-one
or many-to-one mappings. As a result, discriminative neural networks
act as surrogate physical models for forward prediction, making predictions
about the properties of metamaterials based on input feature parameters.
On the other hand, generative networks share the same deep neural
network architecture and neuron-based data processing as discriminative
networks. However, their objective is to learn the distribution of
the training data set and generate new data with additional variations.
This is achieved by mapping input data into a compressed representation
called the “latent space,” from which data similar to
the input can be retrieved.43 Generative
networks are capable of learning the geometric features of data sets
and outputting a distribution of metamaterials layouts.
By employing
discriminative networks such as DNN, it is possible
to construct surrogate models to replace simulation methods like the
finite element method (FEM). This substitution is motivated by the
DNN’s ability to provide accurate predictions of metamaterial
properties with significantly reduced computational time and resource
costs. The foundation of inverse design lies in the forward prediction
enabled by discriminative networks. There are three main pathways
to achieve this goal:
The first approach employs a brute-force
parameter sweeping technique
to search for the desired metamaterial design within a “structure–property”
library. This library is constructed by generating various metamaterial
design protocols supported by surrogate models. However, this method
can become computationally cumbersome when dealing with larger design
spaces.
The second approach integrates discriminative networks
with other
optimization algorithms. The optimization algorithms often necessitate
simulation-based characterization to assess the viability of proposed
metamaterial designs. In this context, discriminative networks function
as surrogate models, effectively supplanting the resource-intensive
simulation processes. Indeed, a more direct avenue is to establish
an inverse discriminative network, wherein the desired material property
serves as the input, and the ensuing output corresponds to the associated
metamaterial geometry. Nevertheless, a challenge arises due to the
nonuniqueness of solutions, where multiple different configurations
of metamaterials can exhibit the same response, resulting in a typical
“one-to-many” problem. This nonuniqueness hinders the
convergence of the neural network training as it violates the uniqueness
of the data set. To address the nonuniqueness problem, the classical
Tandem neural network was invented.44
The third approach hinges upon the utilization of generative networks.
Generative networks autonomously produce new samples in a concise
time frame, thereby enabling the identification of optimal design
strategies from the generated candidates’ pool. Incorporating
an extra condition as an input during the training phase, generative
networks can yield metamaterials designs that align with the desired
response or specific properties.
The AI-based inverse design
of metamaterials not only significantly
improves the efficiency of material development but also provides
new research paradigms. Traditionally, the design of metamaterial
structures relies on theoretical guidance for practical implementation.
Only after fully understanding the relationship between structure
and material response can researchers design specific structures that
meet their requirements. However, for some complex crystals or even
amorphous systems, the well-established description of the correspondence
between structure and response is often lacking. This fact has become
a significant obstacle to the development of metamaterials. By leveraging
AI to design metamaterials, researchers are not required to fully
grasp the intricate relationship between structure and response, enabling
them to bypass the major barrier of theoretical description and directly
predict the optimal structure through data analysis to achieve the
desired functionality. Subsequently, by studying this optimized configuration,
researchers can unveil the inherent relationship between structure
and response in specific physical fields (studying the physical properties
based on the structure is often much simpler than solving its inverse
problem). This, in turn, promotes the development of fundamental physical
theories. Therefore, compared to the dazzling array of novel metamaterials
designed with AI assistance, the profound impact lies in the transformation
of scientific methodology it brings about.
The last couple of
years has witnessed a rapid application of machine
learning to the design of metamaterials ranging from acoustical, electromagnetic,
mechanical, optical, to thermal. There have been already a couple
of review articles in the optical and electromagnetic metamaterials
including the meta surfaces.45−50 Therefore, in this article we focus on the optimization and inverse
design of thermal metamaterials using machine learning techniques,
particularly gradient-free optimization algorithms. The research of
thermal metamaterials has gained a great momentum in past decade,
mainly due to its potential applications in thermal management and
control in microelectronic chips/devices and batteries used in electronic
vehicles.51−54
In this review, we present three distinct pathways that leverage
machine learning to facilitate the optimization and inverse design
of thermal metamaterials:
Optimization of metamaterials using
dedicated optimization algorithms to achieve specific target properties.
Integration of discriminative
models
with optimization algorithms to enhance computational efficiency.
Utilization of generative
models,
including Autoencoder (AE), Variational Autoencoder, Adversarial Autoencoder
(AAE), Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), and other prominent generative
models, to derive the structural information of metamaterials.
More specifically, section 2 will introduce the fundamental algorithms
involved in these
three pathways for designing thermal metamaterials. Section 3 will outline recent advancements
in the applications of machine learning for inverse design and optimization
of thermal metamaterials. Finally, in section 4, we will highlight the principal challenges
encountered and provide suggestions for future research endeavors
in this field.
Artificial intelligence
refers to the capacity of nonanimal entities to mimic or even surpass
certain cognitive abilities of animals, including memory, learning,
communication, perception, reasoning, and problem-solving. AI can
be categorized into two main types: narrow AI and artificial general
intelligence (AGI).55 AGI is also called
Strong AI or Deep AI. AI refers to systems created by humans that
can exhibit intelligent behaviors within a limited range of situations.
However, these systems require human intervention and reprogramming
to adapt to new environmental conditions. On the other hand, AGI represents
more advanced systems that can generalize knowledge and apply it to
novel situations beyond their original scope.56
In AI, machine learning (ML) is a prominent subset that focuses
on developing automated processes enabling machines to learn from
experience, interpret hidden situations, and tackle new challenges.
As learning is a fundamental characteristic of intelligence, ML is
one of the most promising and thriving disciplines within AI.
Machine learning is a scientific approach that employs various
techniques and algorithms to extract knowledge from provided data
and continuously improves its performance through experience. First
proposed by Arthur Samuel in 1952, machine learning has found widespread
applications in diverse fields such as science, technology, engineering,
mathematics, arts, sports, management, economics, and medicine, among
others.57−59
The integration of different ML toolkits has
led to significant
advancements in materials design, enabling the optimization of intriguing
material properties beyond those naturally occurring.60,61
Applications include but not limited to energy materials,62,63 inorganic materials,64,65 perovskites,66 solid-state materials science,67 composite materials,68 metals and alloys,69,70 and polymeric materials.71,72 These applications
have facilitated a deeper understanding of the fundamental chemistry
and physics of materials, while also enabling accurate predictions
of their behaviors.73,74
Incorporating ML techniques into the metamaterials
research can be conceptualized as a cyclic process, as depicted in Figure 1. This process entails
several key stages:
Data acquisition. Data
constitutes a fundamental cornerstone for ML models and must be of
sufficient quantity and quality to effectively address the problem
at hand;
Feature
engineering,
a precursor to the formal integration of ML models, entails the transformation
of data into a suitable format interpretable by computational systems
for ML. The representation of materials encompasses a collection of
variables that delineate distinctive material attributes, referred
to as descriptors;75
Model selection, a
pivotal step in the process, necessitates the identification of candidate
ML methodologies or optimization algorithms. Adhering to the tenets
of the “No Free Lunch Theorems”,76,77 no singular ML algorithm universally outperforms all others across
diverse problem domains. Thus, the task of selecting appropriate models
hinges upon the specific problem context and mandates a meticulous
case-by-case analysis;
Model evaluation ensues,
wherein the performance and efficacy of the chosen models are assessed.
If the selected model yields unsatisfactory results, the preceding
steps are iteratively repeated until a satisfactory solution to the
problem is achieved.

Schematic procedure of machine learning aided design of thermal
metamaterials. It is also applicable to design of other functional
materials.
Both the quantity
and quality of the data set play crucial roles in training a ML model
to reach an accurate/reliable prediction within a reasonable time
frame. Research groups have the option of acquiring data from external
sources or creating their own database. External databases include
but not limited to online resources and/or published literatures,
such as authoritative databases, like Materials Project,78 AFLOWLIB,79 Inorganic
Crystal Structure Database (ICSD),80 Open
Quantum Materials Database (OQMD),81 and
AtomWork.82 However, these public databases
might focus on relatively specific and narrow topics, possibly insufficient
for a comprehensive range of metamaterial design.
Apart from
public materials databases, one may explore data embedded within various
publications. Searching for the required data in this manner, however,
can be time-consuming. Generally, text mining and natural language
processing (NLP) techniques are adapted to extract relevant information
efficiently.
Collecting data from literatures may have a few
drawbacks. First,
the authors might tend to report only their favorite data while disregarding
those seemingly failed data, which can introduce bias into the data
set. Second, experimental data values heavily depend on various experimental
conditions, such as temperature, pressure, humidity, electrical voltage,
etc. Different measurement techniques for the same physical quantity
may yield slightly deviated values, further complicating the performance
of ML models. Hence, databases obtained from other research groups
could be more suitable for researchers to initially assess the feasibility
of their chosen ML models. After filtering out a few models, researchers
can subsequently apply these selected models to their own customized
databases for more targeted investigations. This approach allows researchers
to evaluate the performance and adaptability of ML algorithms using
external data sets before fine-tuning the models on their specific
data.
It would be better for researchers to construct their
own database
through computational simulations and/or experiments. In doing so,
they are not constrained by the availability of pre-existing data
sets. This approach allows for a more comprehensive database, including
“bad” data, and even generating some previously nonexistent
data points. However, building a customized database might be time-consuming,
especially when relying on experimental measurements, which can be
labor and cost intensive. Moreover, computational simulations are
limited by available computational resources and may require substantial
computational time. Nevertheless, investing efforts in creating a
dedicated database can enhance the accuracy and scope of machine learning
applications in metamaterial design.
The collected
raw data must be converted to readable and meaningful representation
for ML models, as ML algorithms prefer specific data forms. The representativeness
of features is critical, as a lack thereof may hinder model convergence
during training, while redundant features can lead to overfitting.
Feature engineering encompasses data preprocessing and feature selection,
both of which play decisive roles in the performance of ML models.
Data preprocessing involves enhancing the integrity, accuracy, and
consistency of the data. Typically, there is a desire to use a smaller
amount of data for model training to reduce computational effort associated
with data set preparation. Despite this, it is essential that the
range of structure parameter values still comprehensively covers the
entire parameter space. Therefore, selecting the most relevant parameters
or variables that can represent response and property features has
become a technical task, which demands expertise of the specific metamaterials
system. Feature selection can be achieved automatically through certain
strategies, such as the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator
(LASSO),83 and the sure independence screening
and sparsifying operator (SISSO).84 For
instance, Hu et al.85 trained the SISSO
model to predict the lattice thermal conductivity across the entirety
of materials within the Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD). The
noteworthy precision achieved in these predictions stands as potential
for identifying materials exhibiting either exceptionally high or
exceedingly low lattice thermal conductivity. These techniques provide
aid in the identification and retention of relevant features, enhancing
the model’s efficiency and effectiveness in handling the data.
A well-prepared data set is paramount for reducing training time
and costs, resulting in a mapping model with minimal errors, thus
aiding researchers in uncovering essential physical and chemical mechanisms.
This prepared data set represents a promising step toward discovery.
Raw data, in contrast, often contains errors, inconsistencies, and
incompleteness, lacking a regular and uniform format. Outliers, which
are data points significantly deviating from predominant patterns,
may need to be removed to enhance prediction accuracy. Handling outliers
is crucial, as they can lead to misleading results during the modeling
process. In the context of metamaterials research, limiting the ranges
of design parameters can be implemented to prevent the emergence of
outliers. Additionally, simulation conditions for numerical characterization
should be set to align with real-world scenarios, further mitigating
the influence of outliers.
Missing data is another common challenge
in real-world data sets
due to physical and artificial limitations in experimental measurements.
For instance, data captured by sensors may have gaps when the sensor
ceases to function for a period, resulting in missing data. To address
this issue, one can replace the missing values with the statistical
mean or median value calculated from the entire data set, thereby
mitigating the impact of missing data on model performance. Moreover,
experimentally obtained data sets might contain noisy data, which
includes meaningless values or incorrect records due to artificial
errors. These noisy values can be treated as null and subsequently
removed from the data set.
In summary, ensuring data quality
through proper data preprocessing,
including handling outliers, missing data, and noisy data, is imperative
for producing reliable and accurate machine learning models in the
context of metamaterials research.
Normalization is a crucial
step in data preprocessing to ensure
that all features of the data set are on a comparable scale, particularly
for algorithms sensitive to input scale variations. Raw data concerning
different design parameters in metamaterials may exhibit varying distribution
ranges. For instance, the height of a unit cell might range from 100
to 300 nm, while the periodicity of the entire pattern spans from
1 to 1.5 μm. To address this, two commonly used scaling approaches
are employed: min-max scaling and standard scaling. Min-max scaling
involves transforming the data to fit within a predefined range, often
between 0 and 1. On the other hand, standard scaling, also known as z-score normalization or standardization, centers the data
so that the mean of the new data set is zero, and the standard deviation
is one. Both normalization techniques assist ML algorithms in converging
more effectively, leading to improved model performance.
Furthermore,
computer vision tasks often necessitate a considerable
number of training images, which can be time-consuming to generate
manually by researchers. To overcome this challenge, data augmentation
techniques are adopted. Data augmentation transforms original images
into multiple variations, effectively increasing the diversity of
the training data set and enhancing the model’s ability to
generalize to unseen data.86
Input
data can take the form of a vector, with each element being
an array of geometrical parameters such as height, width, period,
and diameter.87 Alternatively, it can be
presented as a matrix, with each element representing pixel or binary
values corresponding to the surface of a metamaterial. The output
can be defined as a vector, comprising discretized data points obtained
from a spectrum, such as transmittance. In addition, the output may
represent a specific property value corresponding to a particular
design of metamaterials, such as thermal conductivity. Moreover, the
output could take the form of a matrix that visually depicts the surface
of the metamaterial, produced by generative models. Hence, depending
on the nature of the problem and the data available, ML models for
metamaterials can utilize various input and output representations,
and careful consideration of the appropriate format is essential to
ensure success model training and accurate predictions.
Before inputting
the data into the ML model, the raw data set should be divided into
three distinct subsets: the training set, validation set, and testing
set. The ratio for this division depends on the size of the acquired
database. As a common guideline, the data set is typically divided
into the following manner:88 approximately
80% of the total data constitute the training set, while each of the
validation and testing sets accounts for approximately 10%, respectively.
The training data set is utilized to iteratively update the ML model’s
parameters and establish a mathematical relationship between the metamaterial
design parameters and the corresponding response. The validation set
is used to assess the model’s performance, and its behavior
offers valuable insights for manually tuning hyperparameters. The
testing set comprises samples that were unseen by the ML model during
the training process. These samples serve the purpose of evaluating
the model’s generality and robustness, providing an objective
assessment of the model’s capability to generalize to new and
unseen data. It is assumed that the data within the three subsets
share a common nature, stemming from an identical statistical distribution.
The iterative learning process is executed many times until the model
reaches its ultimate optimization.
There are different model
evaluation metrics in ML models for both classification and regression
problems. For classification problem, accuracy is the most commonly
used evaluation metric. Accuracy represents the fraction of the correctly
predicted samples over the total number of predictions:

used metrics, representing the generalization error and the lower

data, especially abnormal data.

are alternative choices to evaluate the model performance. These functions
can mitigate the data sensitivity, for instance, the Pearson coefficient
