The surface patterns of thermal emitters can be
extended to arbitrary
geometries, and the optimization of surface geometrical topology can
be achieved through machine learning generative models. Kudyshev et
al.310 have adapted the adversarial autoencoder
to improve the optimization process substantially in terms of less
computational time (4900 times faster) and high efficiency (∼98%)
of the thermal emitter with a working band range of 0.5–1.7
μm. The three-layer structure contains a back TiN reflector,
a Si3N4 spacer, and a TiN top layer, which is
defined as the optimization region and discretized into matrix elements,
as shown in Figure 40. The AAE consists of three coupled neural networks: encoder, decoder/generator,
and discriminator. The encoder compresses a given input pattern into
a compact design space, known as a latent space. Subsequently, the
decoder learns to reconstruct the actual input pattern based on a
given latent vector. The AAE performs adversarial learning, similar
to GAN, by incorporating a discriminator to force the latent space
to follow a predefined model distribution. Hence, the AAE can be viewed
as a combination of VAE and GAN. During the training process, the
encoder is trained to perform two key tasks: (i) it takes a 64 ×
64 binary, greyscale image of the top layer as input and compresses
it into a 15-dimensional vector, which represents a position in the
15-dimensional latent space used by the decoder for reconstruction,
and (ii) it generates an extra latent sampling that needs to pass
the evaluation by the discriminator to resemble a sample from the
predefined model distribution. Meanwhile, the decoder functions as
a generator that takes the latent coordinate as input and reconstructs
the design pattern in the real space. Simultaneously, the discriminator
supervises the latent space produced by the encoder to match the predefined
distribution.

AAE-assisted optimization schematics.
Upon completion of training, the decoder operates
as a generator
of new designs. The generated designs are further subjected to refinement
through a filtering process, which eliminates small and sharp features
in the designs produced by the AAE. Subsequently, a pretrained CNN
is employed to predict the efficiency of these emitters (see Figure 41a). For this purpose,
a smaller version of the VGGnet network is selected as the CNN architecture
(see Figure 41b).
The prediction performance of the trained VGGnet regression model
displays r2 = 0.93, indicating a high
accuracy. Remarkably, approximately 88% of the designs generated by
using AAE+VGGnet exhibit high efficiency levels above 80%, with the
best design achieving an impressive efficiency of 95.5%. Moreover,
the optimal generated configuration enables almost all available in-band
emission while effectively suppressing out-of-band radiation. Furthermore,
the AAE+VGGnet approach demonstrates exceptional efficiency by generating
100 highly efficient designs (>80%) within just 2 min, which is
approximately
4900 times faster than using conventional topological optimization
methods. This training process of the AAE enables efficient inverse
design and optimization of thermal emitters with complex surface patterns
and arbitrary geometries. It significantly reduces computational time
while maintaining high optimization efficiency.

(a) Structure refinement
and filtering scheme. The trained AAE
generator is used for design generation, and the proposed designs
are refined with either (i) a topological optimization based approach,
and (ii) the pretrained VGGnet filtering the high efficiency structures.
(b) Schematics of the VGGnet type network used for design efficiency
prediction and robustness classification.
The AAE network can be further extended beyond
random sampling
of designs by incorporating the geometrical parameters of the unit
cell as constraints along with the topology of the emitter’s
surface structure. This type of neural network is referred to as a
conditional adversarial autoencoder (c-AAE). The c-AAE can introduce
physics-driven regularization to compress the design space during
training, leading to improved optimization search.
Kudyshev
et al.311 integrated a c-AAE
with an optimization algorithm to search for the optimal thermal emitter
design with enhanced efficiency. The thermal emitter comprises the
titanium nitride (TiN) back reflector, a silicon nitride (Si3N4) spacer, and a TiN plasmonic antenna in the top layer
(see Figure 42a).
The top antenna image is appended with the spacer thickness and periodicity
of the array to form the input to c-AAE. The primary objective of
the optimization is to find the optimal shape/topology of the top
antenna, the array periodicity, and the spacer thickness, which collectively
result in high emissivity within the working band range of 0.5–1.7
μm. The c-AAE network contains an encoder (E), a decoder/generator (G), and a discriminator
(D), as shown in Figure 42b. The E network compresses
the input design (x) to the 17-dimensional compressed
space, and the coupled G network decompresses the
compressed space back to the original design space. The E and G networks are trained by minimizing the reconstruction
loss between input (x) and generated (x̃) designs. Following training, the G network can
generate new designs given the input compressed space vector z̃ = E(x), which
is a 15-dimensional coordinate vector appended with two conditional
labels l (unit cell size and spacer thickness). To
efficiently evaluate the performance of the generated designs, the
G network is further combined with a conditional Visual Geometry Groupnet
(c-VGGnet) network to estimate the efficiency of the designs based
on the input binary image of the antenna. This avoids the need for
time-consuming full-wave simulations (see Figure 42c). The loss evolution during the training
of the c-VGGnet is displayed in Figure 42d, and the decreasing regression loss indicates
that the c-VGGnet accurately retrieves the efficiency values based
on the input design image. Figure 42e illustrates the comparison between the predicted
efficiency by c-VGGnet and the true values, achieving a sufficiently
high value of r2 = 0.87.

(a) The thermal emitter
design. (b) Training workflow of the c-AAE
network. (c) The trained G network is coupled with
a c-VGGnet for rapid efficiency estimation. (d) Evolution of the training
(blue line) and validation (red line) losses of the c-VGGnet for efficiency
prediction. (e) The regression results performed by c-VGGnet on the
testing data set. White line shows the regression line, and the colormap
shows the number of designs tested. (f) Scheme of the c-AAE based
global optimization algorithm. (g) Spectral emissivity of the best
designs generated by global optimization (red) and randomly generated
(blue). Reproduced with permission from ref (311). Copyright 2021 De Gruyter.
During the optimization process (see Figure 42f), a differential
evolution (DE) optimizer
explores the compressed design space and proposes candidate solutions
to the c-AAE generator. The G network then reconstructs
the design, and the efficiency of the thermal emitter is evaluated
using the c-VGGnet, providing feedback to the optimizer. Based on
this feedback, the optimizer updates its searching parameters for
the subsequent optimization step. This iterative process continues
until the optimal design, hidden within the compressed design space,
is identified. The c-AAE network is then employed to retrieve the
corresponding unit cell configuration of the optimal design. It is
worth highlighting that the proposed approach utilizes a global optimizer
as a black box, offering flexibility to couple the developed c-AAE-based
framework with other optimization techniques. Figure 42g illustrates the efficacy of this approach,
where the red curve represents the absorption spectra of the best
design proposed using the c-AAE-based optimization method, demonstrating
notably high absorption within the working range.
Apart from
TPV systems, thermal emitters find more practical applications
when their emissivity wavelength can be tuned to desired regimes.
For instance, carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless, and tasteless
gas, but it is extremely poisonous to humans being. Therefore, the
development of a low-cost method for CO detection is of paramount
importance. To address this, Granier et al.312 have successfully employed the genetic algorithm for designing an
aperiodic multilayer structure with alternating layers of silicon
and silica on top of a semi-infinite tungsten substrate. The optimized
structure exhibits a narrowband and highly directional emittance at
the frequency λ = 4.7 μm, which corresponds to one of
the molecular resonances of CO. By heating the designed structure,
light is emitted at the resonant frequency of CO (λ = 4.7 μm).
Subsequently, one can use a detector to search for dips in the intensity
of the 4.7 μm light through absorption spectroscopy. Such dips
signify an increase in the concentration of CO in the surrounding
environment, facilitating effective and precise CO detection.
It should be
noted that the optimization of the thermal emitter is only one aspect
of the entire thermophotovoltaic device. Another crucial component
that significantly influences the energy harvesting performance of
the entire system is the thermal absorber. The thermal absorber is
responsible for converting incident solar radiation into thermal energy.
Its efficiency plays a vital role in the overall energy conversion
process. For effective energy harvesting, the thermal absorber needs
to efficiently absorb radiation in the visible and near-infrared (NIR)
range while minimizing emission in the infrared (IR) regime. Achieving
this spectral selectivity often involves modifying the geometrical
parameters of nanostructures within the absorber. Among the various
proposed selective absorbers, those based on multilayer structures
have gained significant interest313,314 because the
number of its potential structure candidates are enormous to be explored
with machine learning method.
Zhou et al.315 have trained the artificial neural network to accelerate
the optimization process of the genetic algorithm searching for an
ultrawideband perfect absorber (UWPAs) from 8 to 14 μm, as shown
in Figure 43a. The
unit cell is a five-layer absorber structure consisting of alternating
thin layers of Ti and GaAs. To improve the convergence rate and prediction
accuracy, the parameters vector and the output absorbance vector are
normalized by the Min-Max scaling method. Note that the neural network
is a surrogate model to predict spectral absorbance given the vector
structure parameters. Input geometrical parameters are the vertical
thickness and the width of each GaAs layer as well as the ratios of
these dimension quantities. Thanks to the neural network, it takes
only 573 s to generate 1.2 × 105 configurations. Compared
with the conventional electromagnetic simulation software (FDTD Solutions),
the computational cost is reduced by 4 orders of magnitude. At normal
incidence, the optimal structure shows four resonant peaks in the
8–14 μm, and the mean absolute errors (MAEs) between
actual and predicted absorbance is only 5.8 × 10–3. Besides, the average absorptance can be maintained to 1 within
the incident angle θ = ±45° and above 0.8 within the
incident angle θ = ±70°. Note that other metamaterial
absorbers cannot keep such a high absorbance under a large incident
angle. The absorbance performance has also been investigated, and
the mechanism turns out to be the strong magnetic field enhancement
generated between different layers at different incident wavelengths.

(a)
Thermal absorber design based on trained neural network to
accelerating the Genetic Algorithm optimization process. (b) Optimization
of thermal absorber by Genetic Algorithm. Reproduced with permission
from ref (316). Copyright
2014 Elsevier.
An artificial solar selective absorber is designed
to efficiently
absorb sunlight while minimizing thermal emission. As a result, the
temperature of the absorber rises during its operation. To ensure
optimal performance at elevated temperatures, tungsten emerges as
a promising candidate material due to its high melting point. Moreover,
tungsten is a refractory metal with high absorption losses in the
visible and near-infrared (NIR) spectral range, making it an excellent
choice for enhancing sunlight absorption. Based on the tungsten–silica
(W-SiO2) cermet as the intermediate layer, Sakurai et al.316 optimized a multilayer selective thermal absorber
by tuning each layer’s thickness and tungsten volume fraction
within the cermet layer through the genetic algorithm, as shown in Figure 43b. They generate
20 initial populations of the absorber structures with various code
strings. Each generated individual is a code string of chromosome
and is assigned the parameters of layer thickness and the metal volution
fractions as the genetic information. During the optimization process,
a pair of elite structures are selected for mating. For the crossover
and mutation operations, part of the code strings is randomly changed
to produce new offspring. After evaluating the Figure of Merit, the
individual with high absorbance is kept as the next generation while
the poor one is discarded. Finally, pick out the best structure at
the termination stage. Their optimal structures with different layer
numbers all achieve solar absorbance of nearly 1, even under the illumination
of a quite low thermal emittance. Therefore, applying the genetic
algorithm directly can solve the optimization problem in designing
thermal absorber.
In another example, Wang et al.317 also
selected tungsten comprising the intermediate layers of a multilayer
thermal absorber. They utilized Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm
to optimize the thicknesses of each layer and experimentally fabricated
the optimal sample by sputtering and chemical vapor deposition techniques
on the wafer scale. The spectral absorbance is validated to be larger
than 0.95 by a Fourier Transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR), under
a low solar emittance that less than 0.1 in the mid-infrared. The
layer composition from top to bottom is: SiO2–Si3N4–W–SiO2–W. They
also selected tungsten as one of the layer materials due to its high
melting point that can make the entire absorber to work at high temperature.
This has been verified by thermal cycling test that the developed
multilayer absorber is thermally stable at 400 °C for up to 72
h heating in air. A Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm is proposed
by Wang et al.318 to optimize the Tamm
emitters. They have achieved a high Q-factor of 508 and an emissivity
peak 0.92 at 4.255 μm, far surpassing the previous results.
Recently, Seo et al.319 utilized a machine
learning surrogate model to optimize the grating structure for a broadband
thermal absorber. The researchers trained a DNN to replace the computationally
intensive rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) method in computational
electrodynamics. By employing the DNN as a surrogate model, they accelerated
the particle swarm optimization algorithm during design process. For
the absorbing material, they chose Cr due to its strong intrinsic
absorption, supporting plasmonic resonance in the visible spectrum.320 The dimensional parameters (i.e., period Λ,
grating width w, grating thickness dg, thickness of topmost SiO2 layer duf, and thickness of bottom SiO2 film dbf) of the grating structure are used as input
layer of the DNN model, as shown in Figure 44a. To train the DNN model, they adopted
the active learning method. They started with an initial data set
of 300 samples and iteratively added 50–100 more samples to
the data set after each validation step until the RMSE was reduced
to a certain criterion value. Ultimately, the DNN model achieved an
impressive RMSE of only 0.003 with a total of 1566 training samples.
The optimized solar absorber design achieved near-unity spectral absorptance
over a wide wavelength range from 400 to 1000 nm (see Figure 44b). The time-saving benefit
of using the DNN model was significant compared to the original RCWA
simulation, with the DNN model requiring less than 0.1 s for estimation
instead of approximately 20 min for RCWA. This substantial reduction
in computation time greatly expedited the entire optimization algorithm,
enabling about 500 million estimations. To validate the optimal design,
the researchers experimentally fabricated a simplified structure by
changing the square hole in the Cr grating to a circular hole. This
simplification was acceptable because the absorptance spectra of the
two structures were nearly identical (see Figure 44c,d), and the measured solar absorptance
of the fabricated optimal design was 0.916.

Cr based grating solar absorber. (b) Absorption
spectra with optimum denoted as red dotted. (c) Original square hole
and simplified circular hole grating structure. (d) Absorption spectra
calculated by RCWA method for fishnet grating structure (blue with

To maximize the evaluation factor of the NFRHT,
Zhang et al.321 employed an adaptive hybrid
Bayesian optimization
algorithm to devise optimal aperiodic multilayer configurations for
both emitter and receiver components. Remarkably, the algorithm achieved
a significantly elevated evaluation factor of 3.98 × 105 W/m2 by examining a mere 2.6% of the samples encompassing
a vast pool of 1.0 × 108 W/m2 candidate
structures drawn from the database. By incorporating the nonvolatile
phase-changing material Ge2Sb2Te5 (GST) for designing the wavelength-selective emitter (Au-GST-Au
configuration), Song et al.322 hybridized
Bayesian optimization with the transfer matrix method, thereby orchestrating
high emissivity within the 5–8 μm wavebands and concomitant
low emissivity within the 3–5 μm and 8–14 μm
regimes. Impressively, this algorithm discerned the optimal structure
by evaluating less than 0.027% of the total candidates, with remarkable
peak emissivity of 0.95 at a wavelength of 5–78 μm.
So far, we have discussed
the separate optimization of thermal emitter or absorber of a TPV
system using machine learning approaches. For a near-field thermophotovoltaic
(NF-TPV), the solar absorber and the thermal emitter are included
in the intermediate structure denoted as the solar transfer section.
Another important subsection of the NF-TPV system is the conversion
section, which is comprised of the thermal emitter and a PV cell.
Therefore, the efficiency of the entire STPV system is calculated
by the multiplication of solar-to-absorber efficiency at the intermediate
layer, and the emitter-to-PV cell efficiency (i.e., PCE). Due to the
tradeoff between solar transfer efficiency and PCE through the emitter
temperature TH at the intermediate structure,
it is difficult to design the PV cell structure to achieve high efficiency
for the entire STPV system. To maximize the efficiency of the entire
STPV system, Song et al.323 have combined
artificial neural network with genetic algorithm to produce optimal
the PV cell design parameters at different emitter temperature TH ranging from 1200 to 2000 K (see Figure 45).
In particular, the PV cell is a multijunction structure, composed
of multiple subcells that are interconnected in series. Each sublayer
is made of GaxIn(1–x)AsySb(1–y) and the combination of x and y determines the bandgap energy. The design variables include
the thickness and bandgap energy of each sublayer, as well as the
emitter temperature TH. The optimal PV
cell can yield the system efficiency of above 25% at 1200 K and higher
than 42% at 2000 K.

Schematic illustration of the multijunction-based
near-field solar
thermophotovoltaic system.
Another application
of selective thermal radiation is radiative cooling, a phenomenon
in which objects cool down by radiating electromagnetic waves. The
Earth’s atmosphere is transparent in the infrared (IR) wavelength
range of 8–13 μm, namely the heat radiation from the
Earth’s surface will go directly to out-space, which acts as
an extensive thermal reservoir because of its low temperature (3 K).
This characteristic facilitates a passive cooling mechanism for terrestrial
bodies at ambient temperature, dissipating heat through radiative
emission. Considering all heat exchange processes (see Figure 46), the net cooling power Pnet of a radiative cooler can be expressed as
where Pr = 2π
∫π/20 sinθ cosθ dθ ∫∞0LBB (Tr,λ) er (λ,θ) dλ is the radiative power emitted
by the radiator, and Pa = 2π ∫π/20 sinθ
cosθ dθ ∫∞0LBB (Tr,λ) er (λ,θ) ea (λ,θ) dλ is the amount of
absorbed incident radiation from atmosphere. The emissivity of the
radiator er (λ,θ) can be defined
by its absorptivity according to the Kirchhoff’s law. The emissivity
of the atmosphere is given by ea (λ,θ)
= 1 – t(λ)1/cosθ, where t(λ) is the atmospheric transmittance in the zenith
direction.324Tr and Ta represent the temperature of
the radiator and ambient temperature, respectively. Pnonrad stands for the nonradiative (i.e., conductive and
convective) heat absorbed by the radiator from the surrounding media. Psolar denotes the absorbed solar power by the
radiator during the daytime. To overcome the adverse effects of solar
radiation, recent advancements in cooling devices have incorporated
features that enable them to function as simultaneous solar reflectors
and IR radiators. These coolers effectively reflect 97% of the incident
solar radiation while still radiating significant IR emission within
the 8–13 μm wavelength range,325 enabling efficient radiative cooling.

cooler. The

To maximize the cooling
rate, a radiative-cooling device must exhibit maximal emissivity within
the spectral range of 8–13 μm. Moreover, for an emitter
designed for daytime cooling, its absorptivity in the visible and
near-infrared range should be minimized to reduce heating from incident
solar radiation. Initially, engineered radiative coolers relied on
simple bulk materials, such as pigmented paints.326 Recent years have witnessed the extension to nanostructured
materials like resonant SiC and SiO2 nanoparticles,327 and the hybrid structure comprising a lossy
photonic crystal reinforced by a thin-film reflector.196 Further development in radiative cooling technology
involved the incorporation of layered systems,197 metasurfaces,328 photonic crystals,329 and hierarchically porous polymer coatings.330
The grating structure has also been applied
to radiative cooling,
in which spontaneous thermal emission from an object exceeds the heat
influx, such as absorption of solar irradiance, nonradiative heat
transfer via conduction and convection.197,331 As shown in Figure 47a,b, Seo et al.332 presented an optimized
complex grating structure using the genetic algorithm, accelerated
through a well-trained ANN. For the grating elements in the hexagonal
array forming the unit cell, SiO2 and Al2O3 were selected due to their high absorption capability and
advantages in systematic lifespan.333 The
incorporation of the surrogate model significantly reduced the computational
time, enabling the prediction of the radiation power of a specific
grating structure in just several milliseconds, compared to one hour
in traditional simulations. The optimal structure resulted in a daytime
radiative cooling power of 89.2 W/m2, associated with a
cooling temperature of 10.1 °C below the ambient temperature
(see Figure 47c,d).
Through finite-difference-time-domain (FDTD) simulations, the researchers
revealed that the electric field was strongly confined around the
SiO2 grating element, while the magnetic field was highly
concentrated inside the SiO2 grating element (see Figure 47e,f). These two
effects resemble the localized surface phonon–polariton and
cavity resonance, which suppress polar-angular sensitivity. The optimal
structure demonstrated promising potential for cold energy harvesting
in plain areas and rooftops of buildings.

Recently, Song et al.334 have undertaken
the design of an optimal surface structure featuring Polydimethylsiloxane
(PDMS) gratings through the amalgamation of a genetic algorithm, facilitated
by an artificial neural network. The culmination of their efforts
has led to the creation of a PDMS grating structure that exhibits
an outstandingly elevated emissivity value achieving 0.99. Notably,
PDMS silicone elastomer stands endowed with promising attributes for
radiative cooling, such as compatible optical properties, ease of
fabrication, and economic affordability.335,336 Nevertheless, their work could be further improved by setting the
radiative cooling power as the objective function rather than the
emissivity to prove the feasibility of PDMS utilized in radiative
cooling. In addition, combining Bayesian optimization with RCWA method
is another efficient approach to achieve radiative cooling, and the
optimal structure can be obtained by calculating only less than 1%
of the total candidate hybrid grading and multilayer structures.337 Besides, Li et al.338 have trained machine learning methodology in concert with the genetic
algorithm to realize daytime radiative cooling. This pioneering undertaking
leveraged a five-layer film structure, whereby the prediction accuracy
of the adeptly trained surrogate model demonstrates an average error
of approximately 0.56%. Moreover, the computational efficiency has
been significantly augmented by the incorporation of the machine learning
model, rendering it 67-fold swifter compared to conventional methodologies
such as the transfer matrix method. The optimal device configuration
demonstrated a noteworthy reduction in ambient temperature by 9.08
°C under steady-state conditions.
Applying the PSO algorithm
directly is another effective approach
to optimize the structural parameters and materials of grating selective
structures, as demonstrated by Zhang et al.339 The design variables include the different materials Mi, the thickness parameters hi, li, and wi, and
the period of the grating selective structure expressed as Λi = li + wi (see Figure 48a). Silver is chosen
as the substrate due to its higher reflectivity in the visible and
near-infrared wavelengths. The net radiative cooling power Pnet is expressed as Pnet = Prad – Psun – Patm – Pnonradiative, where Prad is emissivity power of radiator surface, Psun is absorbed sun power, Patm is the absorbing power of atmospheric thermal radiation, and Pnonradiative are power absorbed by conduction
and convection. In the PSO algorithm (see Figure 48b), each particle represents a solution
with an array of design parameters, and its surface radiation property
is evaluated using the objective function based on Rigorous Coupled-Wave
Analysis (RCWA). The objective function is defined as the difference
between the ideal absorptivity and actual absorptivity in the 0.3–13
μm band, which should be minimized during the optimization process.
Each generation of particles has two optimal solutions: a global optimal
solution found so far and a local optimal solution at that generation.
By comparing these two optimal solutions, the position vector and
velocity vector of each particle are adjusted iteratively. The optimal
structure has achieved a cooling power 72.42 W/m2 during
the day and 121.47 W/m2 at night, when the emitter surface
temperature is equal to the outdoor ambient temperature (see Figure 48c). Its cooling
performance is better than 80% of the flat panel radiator. In addition,
Guo et al.340 designed radiative coolers
using Bayesian optimization and evaluated only less than 1% of the
total candidate structures, as shown in Figure 49. The structure model consisted of polydimethylsiloxane
(PDMS) and five alternating layers of TiO2 and silver.
Bayesian optimization effectively determined the optimal combination
of thickness for each layer.

Compared to previous studies that only geometrical
parameters are
cosidered, the design space can be significantly expanded by incorporating
relevant material properties. Sullivan et al.341 employed a deep neural network as a surrogate model to
explore a library of materials and discover optimal design parameters
for micropyramid structures used in radiative cooling applications.
The output layer of the neural network comprised two neurons to predict
the reflectivity (R) and transmissivity (T), from which the emissivity (ε) can be calculated
as ε = 1 – T – R. The geometry of the micropyramids in Figure 50a, involves three key parameters: the triangle
base span (xspan), height (zspan), and substrate thickness (tsub). In contrast to previous approaches that solely used geometrical
parameters as input, the authors enhanced the neural network input
by incorporating the injection wavelength (λ) and material data
appended to the geometrical parameters. Each wavelength points in
the FDTD simulation had corresponding optical properties linking the
output and material data. Therefore, a single wavelength point was
included as an additional network input. Furthermore, each wavelength
point was associated with refractive index values (n) and extinction coefficients (k), which are related
through the real and imaginary parts of permittivity (εreal and εim). The integration of these correlated
parameters strengthened the connection between input and output, leading
to a higher prediction accuracy (see Figure 50b). The MAE for training and validation
sets are reported as 0.0034 and 0.0035, respectively, and the MSE
for training and validation sets are 0.0034 and 1.53 × 10–4, respectively. The surrogate model can emulate the
FDTD results of over one million distinct combinations in less than
a minute, which is an 8 orders of magnitude improvement. Figure 50c illustrates the
materials and geometries identified by the search process that optimized
the cooling thermal balance at three different surface temperatures:
300 K, 500 K, and 1000 K. The comprehensive incorporation of material
properties and geometrical parameters in the surrogate model enabled
precise predictions, opening new avenues for efficient materials design
and optimization in radiative cooling applications.

The objective
of all scientific research is to advance human well-being
and foster progress in industrial production. Aligned with this fundamental
objective, the in-depth exploration of transformation heat transfer
and thermal metamaterials is motivated by the pursuit of their practical
application and integration into specific engineering challenges.
The design process of thermal metamaterials, characterized by a high
degree of freedom and a lack of strict constraints on target objects,
underscores its unparalleled potential to revolutionize energy utilization.
Additionally, the integration of machine learning techniques into
metamaterial design has demonstrated promising potential, facilitating
exploration within complex design spaces and uncovering novel material
configurations and functions. In section 4.1, we offer a brief outlook on the future
aspects of thermal metamaterials, delving into their design strategies
and real-life applications. Section 4.2 provides a succinct discussion on the
inherent challenges of employing machine learning for metamaterial
design, accompanied by proposed viable solutions to overcome these
obstacles.
Energy and information propagation through networked structures,
such as the metabolism network, neuronal network, porous material
network, etc., have inspired various research in a wide range of fields
such as biology, social science, computer science, and physical science.342−347 A biological neural network controls human intelligence, encompassing
processes such as image recognition, evaluation, thinking, decision-making,
and emotion; all are orchestrated by complex interconnected neuron
networks. It is noteworthy that, akin to electronic devices and battery
systems, maintaining a balanced body temperature around 36 °C
is crucial for our brain and the entire human body. Every aspect of
brain activity entails an energy cost, inevitably resulting in heat
generation and an elevation in the local temperature within the brain.
This necessitates effective heat dissipation through the intricate
neural network of the brain. In analogy to electronic devices, overheating
and abnormal high temperatures concentrated in specific regions could
damage our brain neurons. Conversely, in colder weather conditions,
the human body must efficiently transfer heat into the brain through
its neural network to ensure warmth and the normal functioning of
this vital organ. This delicate interplay underscores the critical
role of the brain’s neural network in maintaining both thermal
equilibrium and optimal functionality under varying environmental
conditions.
The biological evolution of humans, occurring over
millions of years, has finely regulated heat transport in the brain
network, ensuring stability and harmony. Thus, delving into the temperature
distribution and thermal energy manipulation in network structures
could further enhance our understanding of thermal science and contribute
to refined thermal management strategies. We anticipate that such
studies will illuminate novel perspectives in thermal management applications
for the future.
There are multiple thermal properties in our
daily lives, ranging
from thermal insulation to efficient heat dissipation. The former
requires ultralow thermal conductivity, while the latter demands ultrahigh
thermal conductivity.348,349 Complex networks, however, present
a promising avenue for tuning both higher and smaller thermal conductivity,
achieving thermal rectification,350 and
offering potential applications in thermal management. Complex networks
are widely found in natural,351 social,352 biological,353 and
brain systems,354 with their dynamics depending
on the topological structure.355,356 Analyzing the thermal
transport within complex networks can provide practical guidance and
understanding of the thermal conductivity of nanotubes,357−360 the thermoelectric properties of nanotubes,361 energy transport of nanotube,362 thermal conductivity,363−370 and thermoelectric performance371−373 of nanowires, nanofibers,374,375 and polymers,376,377 thereby advancing the preparation
of nanosized devices. The global properties of complex networks are
reflected in their eigenvectors,378 solved
from the network’s Laplacian matrix. The thermal transport
properties of complex networks or network-like structures are affected
by various factors, such as interchain coupling,379 average degree,380 branch, and
density.381 Estimating the energy cost
for upper and lower bounds in complex networks,382 may provide guidance for controlling other devices in science
and engineering.
In essence, the thermal transport behavior
of a complex network
is decisively determined by its Laplacian matrix when its topology
is presented.383 Considering that deep
learning algorithms typically operate on image data sets, which are
converted into RGB-colored matrices (tensors in PyTorch), it is anticipated
that replacing image data with the Laplacian matrix as inputs for
predicting thermal transport properties may enhance the neural network’s
understanding of heat flow mechanisms within complex network structures,
as recently reported by Zhu et al.384 Extending
this philosophy, one may deduce that mechanical response information
is encoded within the dynamical matrix.801 Therefore, it is conceivable to predict the mechanical performance
of a complex network by training a deep learning model with the dynamical
matrix.
Expanding upon the use of the Laplacian matrix as input
for deep
learning, we aim to focus on the thermal conductivity tensor for the
inverse design of thermal metamaterials. This could be achieved through
two pathways. The first approach is to input thermal conductivity
tensor to GAN, VAE, or other generative models. After adequate training,
sampling the latent space could generate the thermal conductivity
tensors, subsequently producing metamaterial structures with desired
thermal properties. An alternative approach involves the application
of optimization algorithms to manipulate the thermal conductivity
tensor, tailoring it for desired functions. We encourage the scientific
community to explore these research avenues collaboratively, fostering
the design of materials and devices that significantly contribute
to the progress of human society. A recent breakthrough by Wei et
al.385 achieving thermal cloak, concentrator,
and rotator through direct topological optimization on the thermal
conductivity tensor, strongly supports the feasibility of our anticipated
approach to treat the thermal conductivity tensor as input for inverse
design.
A complex network can be effectively represented by
a graph, a
data structure defined by a set of nodes and the edges connecting
them. Graphs serve as representations for diverse network structures,
ranging from social media networks to molecular structures, often
encapsulated by their adjacency matrix. Graph Neural Networks (GNN)
emerge as novel models designed for the analysis of graphs, adept
at performing tasks such as node-level, edge-level, and graph-level
predictions. In the context of graph classification, the objective
is to categorize the entire graph into distinct categories. This approach
holds significant promise in various domains where network structures
play a pivotal role. Wang et al.386 employed
Crystal Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (CGCNN) to predict the
thermal conductivities of semiconductors. To enhance prediction accuracy,
they modified the original CGCNN descriptor, denoted as a CGCNN-D
model with an expanded atomic descriptor featuring 58 features, up
from the original nine. Moreover, the thermal conductivity data set
for crystals is relatively small, comprising only 95 semiconductor
single crystals calculated using first-principles theory. To address
this data limitation, transfer learning was adopted. The model was
initially trained on a larger data set of bandgaps with 4160 data
points and then further trained to predict thermal conductivities.
In thermal conductivity prediction, the CGCNN-D model achieved a 10%
reduction in average MAE, and the average R2 increased from 0.874 to 0.904.
Delving into the heat transport
within complex networks holds the
promise of providing valuable research perspectives for manipulating
thermal properties in practical devices characterized by network structures.
Notably, this exploration extends to devices like heat sinks, which
necessitate optimization based on diverse design parameters. As electronic
devices continue to undergo miniaturization, CPU experiences an escalation
in operating power. Additionally, the processing of larger data volumes
by the CPU intensifies heat generation. In contemporary computer manufacturing,
the efficient transfer of this generated heat to the ambient environment
is becoming increasingly challenging. Employing a heat sink has the
potential to augment both the surface contact area between the fins
and coolant and the local mixing velocity of the coolant. Typically,
processors dissipate heat to a heat sink through heat conduction,
followed by transfer to the surroundings through natural, mixed, or
forced convection. The low efficiency of heat removal by the heat
sink poses a potential risk of damage to electronic components as
temperatures rise. The thermal performance of a porous heat sink can
be further optimized by carefully designing the porosity conditions
and geometric parameters of the channel. The optimization of thermal
design for heat sinks aims to minimize both size and weight. Heat
sink shapes range from flat-plate fins to pin-fin heat sinks,387−389 encompassing a diverse set of geometrical parameters, including
the number, thickness, length, and height, inclination angle, and
spacing distance of fins,390−393 the height, width, and shape of the channel,394−396 the location, number, and size of the inlet and outlet.397−399 These parameters hold promise for optimization through machine learning
methods. One may refer to some cited comprehensive reviews for more
details.400−406
Thermal metamaterials and mechanical metamaterials share intriguing
connections and intersections within the realm of advanced material
design. While they operate in distinct domains, the underlying principles
of metamaterial engineering provide a unifying thread that allows
for cross-fertilization of ideas and techniques. They both rely on
the manipulation of microscopic architectures to achieve unique macroscopic
properties. Effective medium theory, often employed in the design
of mechanical metamaterials to predict their mechanical properties,
can also be extended to thermal metamaterials. This theory allows
designers to treat metamaterial structures as homogeneous materials
with effective thermal properties, aiding in the analysis and prediction
of their thermal behavior. Mechanical metamaterials are known for
their ability to control wave propagation and establish phononic bandgaps,
preventing the transmission of specific mechanical waves.407 Many mechanical metamaterials experience changes
in their mechanical properties due to temperature variations, e.g.,
negative thermal expansion. Herein, analyzing mechanical metamaterials
can provide valuable insights and methodologies that can be applied
to the study of thermal metamaterials.
The training of artificial
neural networks relies on specific algorithms and is executed on computers.
Interestingly, the principles of neural network training have sparked
the idea that certain physical entities or systems could also be trained
to perform classification and regression tasks akin to neural networks.
Complex physical networks share structural similarities with neural
networks. In the architecture of a neural network, information enters
the input layer neurons, propagates through the network’s hidden
layers, and ultimately produces signals at the output layer neuron.
By adjusting the number of hidden layers and neurons in the neural
network, the network learns to regulate the weights between interconnected
neurons, enabling the neural network to perform classification and
regression tasks. Analogously, the nodes of complex physical networks
can be viewed as neurons, the strength of connections between nodes
can be quantified by weights. By allowing these complex networks to
autonomously learn and adjust the weights of these connections, they
can exhibit a range of functionalities. Both flow networks and elastic
networks present suitable approaches to accomplish this purpose.
A flow network comprises multiple interconnected nodes (analogous
to neurons) connected by pipes (representing connections). Each node
possesses a specific pressure, and the conductance of each pipe serves
as a trainable parameter that can be adjusted. The nodes are categorized
into three groups: source nodes (neurons in the input layer), hidden
nodes, and target nodes (neurons in the output layer). By enabling
the flow network to autonomously learn and adapt the conductance values
on different pipes, the network can effectively accomplish classification
tasks akin to traditional neural networks.
In 2021, Stern et
al.408 first utilized
a flow network to classify the digits 0 and 1 in the MNIST data set,
as shown in Figure 51a,b. They randomly selected 25 nodes as source nodes and 2 nodes
as target nodes, labeled as 0 and 1, respectively. To classify input
images belonging to digit 0, they required the target node labeled
0 to exhibit high pressure and the target node labeled 1 to exhibit
low pressure. Conversely, for input images belonging to digit 1, the
target node labeled 1 was required to demonstrate high pressure, while
the target node labeled 0 displayed low pressure, as shown in Figure 51c,d. The input
pressure values on source nodes were derived from the 25 principal
components obtained from each image in the MNIST data set using principal
component analysis (PCA). Importantly, it should be noted that the
attainment of the classification function is independent of the specific
structure and topology of the flow network. Any topological pattern
of flow network can achieve classification functionality by simply
adjusting the conductance on each pipe. Furthermore, we can further
anticipate that by altering the number of target nodes to be larger
than two, the flow network can be employed for regression or multiclassification
tasks, thereby enabling a wide range of functionalities. To validate
the trained flow network, experimental implementations were pursued.
Among the possible physics entities for this realization, the resistor
network emerged as the most probable candidate. In this context, the
flow of water inside the pipes in the flow network serves as an analogy
to electric currents. In 2022, Wycoff et al.409 has successfully demonstrated the implementation of this functionality
in experiments using resistor networks.

(a) Untrained disordered
flow network with uniform pipe conductance
identical to 1, indicated by their uniform thickness of green edges.
(b) Trained flow network by modifying their conductance. (c,d) Response
of the network with input image at the top left. The pressures of
the target nodes labeled as blue 0 and black 1 circle. Reproduced
with permission from ref (408). Copyright 2021 American Physical Society.
An elastic network is comprised of interconnected
nodes and springs,
which create diverse geometric configurations capable of sustaining
multiple stable states (see Figure 52a). These stable states can be harnessed to achieve
neural network-like classification tasks. By introducing perturbations
to the positions of individual nodes, the elastic network can fall
into to one of its stable states (see Figure 52b).

(a) Continual learning for storing multiple
stable configurations.
The networks grow incrementally during learning, and new bonds are
created in one iteration step. (b) Elastic network composed with nonlinear
springs can store two states in energy landscape. (c) Training images
from MNIST database. (d) Test images that trained network has never
seen before. (e) Classification results of nonlinear elastic network
can distinguish between images of number 0 and 1. Reproduced with
permission from ref (410). Copyright 2020 American Physical Society.
Stern et al.410 developed
an elastic
network with multiple stable states to execute the binary classification
task for digits 0 and 1 in the MNIST data set. During the training
process, the learnable parameters encompass the node positions and
nonlinear elasticity constants between nodes. Converting pixel grayscale
values of an image into 400 node positions, relaxed springs are established
between nodes within a specific threshold distance, and the elasticity
constants of these springs are increased at a certain rate. When presented
with a new image, the nodes are repositioned based on the grayscale
values, and the springs generated from the previous image are retained,
while new relaxed springs are generated in the same way. This ongoing
process of “continue learning” allows the elastic network
to accumulate new stable states while preserving the existing ones.
As the nodes’ positions are altered, they converge to one of
the stable states stored during learning. Subsequently, when a test
set image of 0 or 1 is provided, the trained network correctly identifies
and classifies the image’s category (see Figure 52c–e).
Furthermore,
we speculate that the allosteric response of an elastic
network could also emulate the classification and regression functionalities
of a neural network. The elasticity constant of the springs can be
adjusted through learning, analogous to the modulation of weights
between neurons’ connections in a neural network. In the elastic
network, when certain nodes are stimulated by an external strain,
other nodes will also perform a certain degree of strain. Eventually,
each node will move to a position of force balance. Regarding the
strain on source nodes as input, the response strains on the target
nodes are treated as outputs. Similarly, the remaining nodes are analogous
to hidden layers of neural networks. By selecting specific nodes as
source and target nodes, and subjecting the source nodes to specific
strains while minimizing the disparity between the strain experienced
by the target nodes and the desired strain, the elasticity constants
of each spring in the network can be tailored. In this manner, the
elastic network can achieve neural network-like functionalities. This
kind of research has the potential to advance the field of biophysics.
As a type of mechanical metamaterial, origami sheets exhibit capabilities
akin to training neural networks, enabling them to achieve classification
and regression functionalities (see Figure 53). By subjecting an origami sheet to a specific
force pattern, it can be folded into a distinct shape. Different force
patterns lead to diverse folded configurations. Analogously, we can
treat the applied strain as the input of a neural network, while the
resulting folded geometric configuration represents the network’s
output. When the applied force pattern arises from two distinct classes,
and the origami sheet folds into only two configurations corresponding
to these force patterns, we can employ the origami sheet as an alternative
to a neural network for classification tasks. However, a challenge
arises from the fact that different force patterns often lead to different
folded configurations. To overcome this issue, Stern et al.411 pioneered training an origami sheet to accomplish
a classification task by adjusting the stiffnesses of creases on the
sheet. They utilized a training data set comprising images of cats
and dogs. On the sheet, they selected specific creases to apply external
forces, where each crease had a different stiffness. The crease stiffness
represents the resistance strength to external forces, with higher
stiffness making it more difficult for external forces to alter the
structure. Therefore, during the learning process, the stiffness of
different creases can be adjusted, analogous to tuning the weights
in a neural network. Ultimately, after training, when a force pattern
derived from cat images is applied to the well-trained origami sheet,
it folds into a specific configuration. Similarly, when a force pattern
from the dog image class is used, it folds into another specific configuration.
This highlights the origami sheet’s ability to perform image
classification tasks. To achieve this, the gray scale values of each
pixel in the image are converted into strains applied to the creases.
Similar to reducing the loss function in a neural network, the origami
sheet adapts the stiffnesses of different creases for different categories
of input images. This helps facilitate the sheet’s folding
into the corresponding structure.

A thin, stiff origami sheet with creases
whose stiffnesses can
be changed by repeated folding. The sheet can fold in response to
the discrete spatial force pattern applied on the sheet. A trained
sheet classifies force patterns by showing one distinct folded response
for each class.
Implementing the origami classification task through
experiments
presents several challenges. First, during the preparation phase,
achieving varying stiffness for different creases on the origami sheet
requires precise control and can be labor-intensive. Manually folding
origami sheets to meet specific stiffness requirements may be difficult
to accomplish accurately. Second, in the testing phase, uneven distribution
of strains applied to different creases makes the design of devices
for applying external forces challenging. This nonuniform strain distribution
further complicates the experimental setup. Nevertheless, our motivation
for exploring physical systems as alternatives to neural networks
for achieving classification functionalities stems from the higher
feasibility of their experimental implementation. Utilizing physical
entities in lieu of neural networks holds tremendous potential for
driving advancements in the discovery and development of new materials,
as well as enabling revolutionary technological breakthroughs. The
ability to execute these experiments empowers researchers to explore
and exploit the unique characteristics of physical systems, which
may lead to novel insights and innovative solutions in the field of
metamaterials and beyond.
Electronic devices are a collection of integrated devices designed
to regulate electric current flow for various applications including
motion control and information processing. In recent decades, the
electronic performance of these devices has been enhanced through
the integration of more and miniaturized components. This rapid development
has encountered a bottleneck, the so-called “heat death”
problem in the semiconductor industry. Namely, the fast and powerful
electronic device will generate a large amount of heat due to joule
heating that will lead to the accumulation and temperature rise locally
(hot spot) if the heat is not dissipated timely. The temperature rise
will eventually lead to a breakdown of the device. Generally, each
device operates within a specific temperature range, for example,
an electronic device is between 85 and 100 °C, whereas the battery
for electronic vehicles between 15 and 35 °C. Beyond the range,
the reliability of the device undergoes a sharp deterioration.412−414 Research findings show that for every 1 °C increase above the
specified limit temperature, the chip’s reliability decreases
by 5%, leading to a substantial reduction in its lifespan.415 Therefore, an efficient thermal management
system is crucial to guarantee the electronic devices operating steadily
and efficiently.416 Thermal management
in electronics encompasses a wide range of spatial and temporal scales,
spanning from nano- and microscale hotspot mitigation on chips to
macroscale cooling in data center infrastructure.417 By controlling the direction and magnitude of thermal flux,
thermal metamaterials hold significant potential for applications
in the thermal management of electronic devices.418−421
In practical usage, various electronic components are interconnected
on a printed circuit board (PCB). As reported by Dede et al.,422 thermal metamaterials, including thermal cloak,
concentrator, and rotator, can be integrated within the printed circuit
board to delineate a hot spot region and a temperature-sensitive device
region. To strategically position thermally sensitive elements, electronic
circuits, components, or systems, considerations are given to locating
them in regions with minimal thermal disturbances. This entails arranging
them where the thermal gradient across the elements is as close to
zero as possible, irrespective of temperature variations in the surroundings.
To prevent direct thermal contact between the heat-generating device
and the temperature-sensitive device, a cloak is employed.423 Subsequently, a thermal rotator is applied
to redirect the heat flow around the temperature-sensitive device
toward the cooler end of the PCB. Meanwhile, a thermal concentrator
embedded at the coldest portion of the PCB collects heat from the
temperature-sensitive device, further reducing its temperature. The
thermal concentrator also holds promise for thermal energy harvesting,
maximizing limited temperature differentials relative to the ambient
environment for thermoelectric generators.424 Additionally, the thermal rotator can distort and guide the heat
flow toward a heat sink, enhancing heat dissipation efficiency. Interested
readers can refer to highlighted references for further exploration.425−428 Besides, thermal camouflage has been optimized to conceal the thermal
signature of the targeted electronic equipment serving as a heat source
by dissipating heat from the target to reduce its temperature.429 Shen et al.430 introduced
a thermal converger that enables the design of a thermal grating,
effectively concentrating and focusing heat with high efficiency for
subsequent energy conversion.
Beyond the realm of passive thermal
metamaterials designed to manipulate
the direction of heat flow, future research is poised to explore active
thermal metamaterial devices. In practical terms, it illuminates the
development of thermal devices that regulate heat flow analogous to
how electronic devices,431 such as diodes
and transistors,432−436 control electric current. The fundamental thermal device in this
context is the thermal diode, serving as a one-way traffic road for
heat flow.437 Essentially, it permits heat
flow in one direction while inhibiting it in the opposite direction.
Leveraging temperature-dependent conductivity for the design of switchable
thermal cloaking is one such avenue, which could be utilized for the
creation of a macroscopic thermal diode.191 For some phase change materials, their thermal conductivities depend
on temperature. This temperature dependence can be used to build thermal
diodes, regulators, and switches.438 Nevertheless,
discovering materials with a robust temperature-dependent thermal
conductivity in nature is challenging. Shape-memory alloys, renowned
for their near-room-temperature phase transition point and customizable
deformation patterns, find widespread use in crafting thermal switches
and diodes. These advancements hold the potential to open new avenues
for temperature control and dynamic thermal management in electronic
packaging.439
It is envisaged that
the design of a self-adaptive thermal metamaterial
for manipulating the thermal field holds great promise for future
studies. In a recent development, Jin et al.440 trained an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to autonomously control
the rotating angular velocity of a bilayer structure. This control
aimed to further manipulate the effective thermal conductivity and,
consequently, the temperature gradient within the targeted region.
Notably, this automatic control has been successfully demonstrated
in hardware implementation by integrating the pretrained ANN into
a Raspberry Pi microcomputer. The ANN, upon detecting the ambient
temperature and receiving input from a microinfrared camera, can regulate
the rotating speed of PDMS through a stepper-motor driver. This work
represents a novel approach to thermal management in chips and other
related areas.
When incorporating thermal metamaterials in heat
flow manipulation
of electronics, researchers and engineers need to consider several
crucial aspects. First, attention must be paid to the thermal and
mechanical alterations in nanosized metamaterials when subjected to
significant deformation.441 Deformation
is often an unavoidable aspect in the practical application of devices.
Numerous studies have emphasized the substantial impact of deformation
on the thermal conductivity of nanostructures,442−445 although some debates exist, suggesting minor effects under small
strains.446,447 Thus, further investigations
are warranted to explore the implications of deformation on heat management
devices utilizing metamaterials. Second, selecting appropriate materials
for thermal metamaterial requires careful consideration. To circumvent
potential thermal expansion and long-term interfaces issue, homogeneous
materials may be preferred. Additionally, materials with well-defined
geometric structures that are easily fabricated or manufactured would
provide additional practical advantages. Finally, we anticipate that
future research will delve into system-level studies, focusing on
the implementation of thermal metamaterials in the context of 5G and/or
6G-related communications.
Based on
whether a certain machine learning algorithm requires an external
interpreter to understand their decision-making mechanisms, models
can be broadly categorized as either “white-box” or
“black-box” models. “White-box” models
are algorithmically interpretable, meaning they do not need an external
interpreter to reveal the rationale behind their decision-making process.
On the other hand, “black-box” models rely on additional
explanation to elucidate their internal logic, as their decision-making
processes are not readily transparent. Only a limited subset of machine
learning models is considered intrinsically interpretable, which includes
linear regression, naive Bayes, decision trees, and other tree-based
models like Random Forest. Linear models learn a series of coefficients
that yield a weighted sum for making predictions. These coefficients
can be interpreted as scores for evaluating the importance of features.
While surrogate models are predictive, many of them lack interpretable
mechanisms that elucidate the mapping relationships between metamaterial
properties and descriptors.448 Uncovering
the computational “black box” underlying the fitting
process can help scientists in efficiently designing metamaterials
with desired targets, constructing descriptors following a more logical
pathway, and gaining a better understanding of the underlying physical
properties. This understanding has the potential to significantly
enhance the research and development of metamaterials.
Although linear regression and decision tree algorithms
are considered interpretable and offer global interpretations, they
may fall short in capturing complex feature-property relationships,
particularly when faced with nonlinear relationships. Despite extensive
regularization efforts, linear models cannot adequately explain nonlinear
connections. To address these limitations and enable the interpretation
of nonlinear models, novel methods have emerged. One widely used approach
is permutation feature importance, which assesses a feature’s
significance by measuring the increase in model error after permuting
that specific feature.449 This method is
characterized by its speed, ease of comprehension, and capacity to
provide global interpretations for a broad spectrum of nonlinear relationships.
However, it may exhibit bias when dealing with correlated features,
lacks the ability to illustrate the effects of features on predicted
values, and its reproducibility may be affected by the randomness
introduced during calculation.
Another popular method is Shapley
additive explanation (SHAP).450 SHAP aims
to measure the contribution of each feature to the prediction of an
individual sample, seeking to generate global interpretations that
often encompass a range of values and signs, as feature importance
becomes a local property for nonlinear models.451 SHAP decomposes the model output by summing the impact
of each feature, based on the concept of Shapley values derived from
game theory, to calculate the contribution of each feature to the
model outcome. Notably, SHAP not only analyzes the importance of each
feature but also serves as a visualization tool, making machine learning
models intuitively explainable by visually representing their output.
For example, as illustrated in Figure 54, the red area represents the positive contribution
of a feature that enhances the predictive value of the model, while
the blue area signifies the negative contribution of the feature.
The final output prediction value is a cumulative summation of the
contributions from all features. This visualization makes predictions
more comprehensible for researchers who are not well-versed in machine
learning models. However, it is crucial to exercise caution when using
SHAP, as it may yield unreliable results when dealing with correlated
features, necessitating careful examination by domain specialists.
Despite this limitation, SHAP remains a valuable and powerful tool
for understanding and interpreting the complex workings of nonlinear
machine learning models.

Schematics of SHAP framework.
While ML based models have proven valuable in the inverse design
and optimization of targeted properties for metamaterials, understanding
the underlying physics governing the structure–property relationship
remains challenging. However, an alternative perspective could be
considered: Can ML models be employed to identify a set of design
parameters that exert a dominant impact on the properties of metamaterials?
By identifying key design parameters, it becomes possible to flexibly
adjust the target property to a wide range of desired values, presenting
an indirect approach to tackling the inverse design problem. This
can be achieved by dimensionality reduction function of a variety
of neural network structures. Several studies have utilized techniques
such as autoencoders, variational autoencoders, and other neural network
structures with dimensionality reduction functions to unveil essential
geometrical parameters that significantly influence the response of
metamaterials. The fundamental concept involves analyzing the weights
associated with the bottleneck layer of the autoencoder. In essence,
this approach seeks to distill the crucial design parameters from
the complex metamaterial data, providing valuable insights into the
most influential factors affecting the required properties. By understanding
and grasping these key design parameters, researchers can make informed
decisions in metamaterial design, leading to enhanced control and
tailoring of the electromagnetic response for a variety of applications.
Dimensionality reduction is a crucial technique for extracting
essential design parameters that exert significant influence on the
properties of metamaterials. Within the framework of deep learning
networks, autoencoders offer an effective means of achieving dimensionality
reduction through their encoder part. By observing the summation of
weights among the neurons at the bottleneck layer of the autoencoder,
one can identify the design parameters that contribute most to the
output response. These extracted parameters not only enhance the efficiency
of inverse design but also provide researchers with a deeper understanding
of the underlying mechanisms governing the responses of metamaterial
properties. A prominent feature of autoencoder is that the input is
identical to the output. Assume a spectrum vector is input into the
autoencoder, it undergoes dimensionality reduction at the bottleneck
layer and subsequently recovers the spectral property at the output
layer. Kiarashinejad et al.452 reported
that combined with a pseudoencoder, an autoencoder can extract the
essential design parameter governing the absorption response of an
optimal metasurface light absorber. The 3D metasurface was constructed
by the periodic arrangement of a supercell, described by 10 design
parameters, as depicted in Figure 55a. In the first step, the autoencoder is trained to
reduce the original response space, as shown in Figure 55b. Subsequently, a pseudoencoder
was employed to reduce the original design space to a reduced design
space, which was then mapped with the reduced response space, as illustrated
in Figure 55c. The
term “pseudoencoder” arises from the fact that its input
and outputs are derived from different spaces. Specifically, the input
originates from the design space, while the output is obtained from
the reduced response space. An additional neural network, which colored
by purple neurons, was introduced to establish a relationship between
the original response space and the reduced design space by cascading
the encoder network in the autoencoder with the reduced design space,
as shown in Figure 55c. In Figure 55d,
the pseudoencoder effectively reduces the original 10 design parameters
to 4 reduced spaces, with green and red arrows denoting positive and
negative weights, respectively. Each weight is multiplied by its corresponding
design parameter and transmitted to the bottleneck layer. Figure 55e displays the
weights values, where larger weights indicate a stronger contribution
of the corresponding parameter. The thickness of the arrows connecting
the nodes between the input and bottleneck layers in further Figure 55d illustrates this
strength. As depicted in Figure 55h, the parameter “height” (h) emerges as the most vital design parameter, as it connects to all
4 nodes in the bottleneck layer, displaying strong weights. Consequently,
the response space is more sensitive to changes in the height parameter
(h). To confirm the significance of the height parameter, Figure 55f presents the
COMSOL simulation results when varying the height while keeping the
other 9 design parameters fixed. The substantial variation range in
the response highlights the pivotal role of the height parameter in
influencing the metasurface light absorber’s performance.

(a)
3D representation of metasurface. (b) Autoencoder structure
for dimensionality reduction technique. Autoencoder is used to reduce
the dimensionality of the response space. (c) The pseudoencoder relates
the original design space to the reduced response space while reducing
the dimensionality of the design space. (d) The pseudoencoder architecture
relating the original design space to the reduced response space through
reducing the dimensionality of the design space. Weights in a color
map for the reduced design space. (e) Strength of the weights which
are connected to different design parameters. (f) Variation of the
response using COMSOL where h varies and other parameters
are fixed. Reproduced with permission from ref (452). Copyright 2020 Springer.
Upon extracting the essential design parameters
through the dimensionality
reduction capability of the autoencoder, it becomes possible to precisely
tailor the response of metamaterials to the desired target over a
wide range. Hemmatyar et al.453 employed
the autoencoder and pseudoencoder to design and experimentally realize
an all-dielectric metasurface (MS) capable of generating a broad color
range. The metasurface consists of HfO2 nanopillars with
height (h) and diameter (d) deposited
on a SiO2 substrate, forming multiple square lattices with
periodicity (p), thus comprising three design parameters
(see Figure 56a).
A data set of 2000 square-lattice structures was generated, and their
reflectance spectra were characterized using the finite-difference
time-domain (FDTD) technique. The square-lattice parameters served
as the design space, while the reflectance spectra constituted the
response space. In the first step of training, an autoencoder neural
network was trained to reduce the dimensionality of the original response
space (dimensionality of 200) to a reduced response space (referred
to as the bottleneck layer) with a dimension of 7 and then recover
the original response features (again with a dimension of 200). Subsequently,
a pseudoencoder was employed to reduce the dimensionality of the original
design space (with a dimension of 3) to a reduced design space (with
a dimension of 2) and generate output to match the reduced response
space (with a dimension of 7). The reduced design space, also known
as the bottleneck layer, is the second hidden layer of the pseudoencoder.
By analyzing the weighting coefficients relating the first and second
layers of the pseudoencoder, the role of different design parameters
in influencing the response of the unit cell was revealed, as shown
in Figure 56b. Each
sector illustrates the weights of the first layer to each node in
the second layer (i.e., bottleneck), indicating the contribution of
each design parameter to the latent features. Notably, the periodicity
emerged as the most dominant parameter in altering the latent features
and, consequently, changing the output response. The output response
displayed a high sensitivity to the periodicity. Accordingly, by varying
the periodicity, the position of Fano-type resonance could be readily
adjusted, leading to the induction of different colors across the
entire visible range. Ultimately, by changing the periodicity of the
lattices from p = 270 nm to p =
450 nm, a wide color range was achieved, and the results were experimentally
validated using electron-beam resist (EBR), electron-beam lithography
(EBL), and atomic layer deposition (ALD) to fabricate the metasurface.
Parts c and d of Figure 56 demonstrate that a diverse range of colors was successfully
realized, with the simulation and experimental data showing good agreement.

Schematic of all-dielectric metasurface composed of HfO2 nanopillars fabricated on a SiO2 substrate. (b)

the reflectance response and generated colors. Strength of each design
