The concept of
cloaking, which involves masking objects from detection, has garnered
significant attention in recent years. Metamaterials, being continuous
in their design space, offer versatile possibilities through various
generation approaches. In contrast, natural materials are relatively
discrete in their design space due to limitations in chemical composition
and charges, making the arbitrary integration challenging. Consequently,
machine learning models are well-suited for metamaterials design.
Artificial neural networks are commonly employed as alternative models
for physics simulations. Their advantage lies in their rapid evaluation
when properly trained, compared to traditional numerical simulation
computations. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that this surrogate
model merely serves as an approximation to the real physics model,
which can lead to systematic errors. Consequently, it is highly recommended
to verify the prediction results obtained from the surrogate model
through physical calculations before undertaking any subsequent actions,
such as fabrication of the designed structure and experimental validation.
Neglecting the validation of the actual properties or responses of
the optimized metamaterial design can lead to wasted time/funding,
and effort in reckless experimental fabrication. Particularly at singular
points, the surrogate model’s error can become orders of magnitude
higher. Therefore, it becomes essential to ascertain whether the property
predicted by the surrogate model is valid or merely a result of a
singularity in the design space.233 Prudent
validation ensures the reliability and accuracy of the predictions,
reducing the risk of erroneous conclusions or misinformed decisions
in metamaterial design and fabrication.
Ji et al.234 have designed and experimentally realized a
multilayer thermal cloak device using an artificial neural network
and a brute force searching method. The device is composed of five
layers with equal lengths but different thermal conductivities, which
are the design space to be optimized by machine learning (see Figure 19a). The neural
network is trained adequately to predict the relationship between
design parameters and the thermal cloak performance using it as a
surrogate model (see Figure 19b). Then they used this surrogate model directly to generate
another 10 000 candidate designs and the optimal cloak device
is searched among these samples. Note that the generation process
is completed within 76 s, which is highly improved compared with calculation
using the Finite Element Analysis of around 13 min. It is worth pointing
out that their optimal device is experimentally fabricated and validated.

To obtain the different thermal conductivities
of every layer,
they prepare the composite structures by drilling holes into the copper
plate and filling them with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Both the
experimental and simulation results show excellent agreement, and
the optimal thermal cloak can guide the heat flows to pass around
the domain and return to their original flow paths without invasion
(see Figure 19c,d).
However, to achieve the inverse design for cloak structures, an exhaustive
search across the extensive parameter space becomes imperative. As
evidenced by their exploration of an additional 10 000 candidates,
it is evident that discovering the ideal metamaterial structure requires
further searching due to the need to identify the required material
amidst a substantial pool of candidates. To expedite this process,
it is desirable to directly input the target property or response
into the neural network, enabling the network to propose a candidate
structure that meets the specified criteria. This objective can be
realized through the utilization of more advanced network structures,
such as autoencoders. By leveraging autoencoders, the design process
can be enhanced through the extraction of essential features and reduction
of input data dimensionality, facilitating faster exploration within
the parameter space.
Wang et al.235 have employed a conditional
variational autoencoder (cVAE), a type of generative network, to accomplish
the inverse design of a thermal cloak with arbitrary geometry. They
constructed a data set by generating a set of topological functional
cells (TFCs) labeled with the effective thermal conductivity tensor κ′, as depicted in Figure 20a. The architecture of the generative model
is illustrated in Figure 20b,c, where the encoder compresses the input image of the unit
cell into a latent space, while the decoder reconstructs the input
image from the latent variable. During the training process, the authors
incorporated the effective thermal conductivity tensor as a label
along with each input unit cell, leading to the “condition”
term in the model (see Figure 20d). Upon completion of the training, inputting a specific
sampling point with the desired thermal conductivity tensor into the
decoder, it can generate a new reconstructed microstructure. By tessellating
these microstructures, the final macroscopic thermal cloak device
is obtained. Two of the designed cloak devices were experimentally
realized by the authors, as depicted in Figure 20e,f. The results indicate that the temperature
field inside the object region remained constant, while the external
temperature field of the background remains largely unaffected, confirming
the successful implementation of thermal cloaking functionality.

(a)
The predesigned unit cell data set. (b) Architecture of the
deep generative network. (c) Distribution of training data in latent
space. (d) The microstructure coupled with label is encoded into latent
space, and the decoder samples from a latent variable to generate
the microstructure with target thermal property. (e,f) Experimentally
measured temperature fields of two thermal cloaks. Reproduced with
permission from ref (235). Copyright 2023 John Wiley & Sons.
In their work, the encoder and decoder comprised
a series of building
blocks involving 2-dimensional convolutional layers, distinguishing
it from the original autoencoder network structure, where the intermediate
layers are 1-dimensional neural networks. The VAE model and its derived
cVAE model effectively solved the many-to-one problem when compared
with the utilization of the inverse discriminative model. Additionally,
the dimensionality reduction performed by their encoder network revealed
the essential and independent variables in the input descriptors.
However, it is worth noting that the dimensionality of the latent
space itself is a tunable hyperparameter, requiring manual adjustment
in multiple training iterations. Consequently, the first epoch of
training might not yield the best results, a careful parameter tuning
during the model development process is necessary.
Alternatively,
another viable approach involves the direct utilization
of evolutionary algorithms to design the optimal cloaking structure.
Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm has been validated to achieve
thermal cloak in a multilayer device as well, reported by Alekseev
et al.236 in 2019. In their work, the cloak
domain is a cylindrical layered shell consisting of M homogeneous isotropic layers. The thermal conductivity
of each layer kj is a
diagonal tensor in polar coordinates r,θ and
its diagonal components krj and kθj (j = 1,2, . . .,M, j represents the layer index) are all the positive values. The combination
of these diagonal components of each layer forms a 2M-dimensional
vector k = (kr1,kθ1, . . .,krM, kθM) and finding
an optimal k can tune the entire thermal
conductivity of the domain Ω to achieve thermal cloak (see Figure 21a). A finite set
of vectors in the design space k1, . . .,kN are regarded as particles in the Particle Swarm Optimization
algorithm. During optimization, one sets of the initial swarm positions
are iteratively updated by ki+1j = kijvij for all particles kj, where j denotes
the particle number j = 1, . . .,N and i indicates the iteration number. The velocities vij of these particles to change
their motion are also updated by:
where w, c1, c2 are constant parameters; d1 and d2 are random
variables that are uniformly distributed over the interval (0, 1); pj and pg are the personal
best for each particle and global best for the entire swarm. The optimization
problem for this algorithm is actually to minimize a cost functional
that depends on the conductivity vector k. They have defined two cost functionals Je(k) for external domain Ωe and Ji (k) to describe the internal domain Ωi. The definition of cost functionals are
defined from the cloak properties of these domains. For an ideal cloak,
one condition is that the temperature difference between the cloak
region Ω and external region Ωe is minimal,
and this is described by cost functional Je(k). The second cloak condition is that the temperature
is constant inside the cloak region Ωi, so the temperature gradient equals zero, and this is where
the cost functional Ji(k) originates from. The optimization cloak design
is shown in Figure 21b. It is noticed that inside the cloak region, the temperature distribution
is constant and the isolines outside the cloak region are not distorted,
implying that the Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm realizes a
perfect cloak function. Recently, PSO has also been applied to design
a bilayer thermal sensor.237 The combination
of PSO and the finite element method offers noteworthy advantages
owing to its wide-ranging applicability that covers two aspects. First,
this approach demonstrates versatility in optimizing various shapes
and external fields of alternating layers. It can effectively handle
complex geometries and diverse external conditions. Second, the methodology
exhibits adaptability by easily addressing problems related to thermal
concentration and rotation. This can be achieved by making modifications
to the objective function, enabling efficient optimization for specific
requirements and constraints.

Swarm Optimization algorithm. (b) Isolines of temperature field for

Ji et al.238 have trained an artificial neural network as
a surrogate model to map the relationship between four design parameters
and the thermal concentration performance, as shown in Figure 22a. Their primary objective
was to explore the optimal tangential and radial heat conductivities kθ′ and kr′ of the shell region, which are determined
by its structural parameters. Given the design space D = [d1, d2, d3, d4]
as the input layer, the artificial neural network has been trained
to accurately predict conductivities k1 and k2. During the training process,
1000 samples from training data set are used to minimize the objective
function E(k1, k2; α,β) = α|k1 – kθ′|
+ β|k2 – kr′|, and the training process
is supervised by the mean square error  between predicted values Ê and real values E. An additional 200 samples from
the validation data set were utilized to avoid overfitting, while
300 samples from the testing data set were employed to assess the
prediction accuracy of the network. The trained network demonstrated
high prediction accuracy, as evidenced by the small values of relative
errors (see Figure 22b,c). Subsequently, the researchers generated 10 000 new samples
and utilized the well-trained network to identify the optimal design
parameters for the thermal concentrator. The experimentally realized
device effectively focused the heat flux into its central region while
maintaining the thermal field outside the device unaffected (see Figure 22d–f). This
approach can be further extended to manipulate other diffusion (e.g.,
mass) or wave fields (e.g., acoustic and hydrodynamic) governed by
linear partial differential equations. Furthermore, the relationship
mapping the design variables and effective thermal conductivities k1 and k1 by neural
network can also be used as a surrogate model to accelerate the optimization
design process of the genetic algorithm in developing the thermal
harvesting devices, as reported by Ji et al.239 Compared with the temperature fields between ideal case and proposed
thermal harvesting device, the genetic algorithm has achieved heat
energy harvesting into the central region without much disturbance
of the external thermal field (see Figure 23a,b). The proposed device was practically
fabricated using copper, demonstrating thermal gradients characterized
by ΔTin = |Ex=r1 – Tx=–r1| twice as large as in the contrast plate (see Figure 23c).

Although constructing the pattern-property library
and searching
for the desired design offer potential benefits, their applicability
in every scenario is not guaranteed. Several challenges need to be
addressed. First, the prediction accuracy achieved within the testing
data set may not necessarily extend to predictions outside the data
set scope, particularly when seeking optimal designs within the entire
parameter space. The substantial parameter space demands careful consideration
and thorough exploration to ensure reliable results. Second, creating
a library encompassing every design candidate can be computationally
demanding, considering the vastness of the parameter space. Additionally,
to build an accurate surrogate model, thousands of iterative loops
and intermediate computation steps are typically required during the
training process, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive.
Moreover, it is essential to recognize that the surrogate model remains
an approximation of the actual physics properties of metamaterials,
leading to the introduction of systematic errors. Therefore, it is
imperative to validate the actual properties of the inversely designed
metamaterials through computational simulation to ensure their reliability
and accuracy. Considering these challenges and drawbacks, researchers
must exercise caution and conduct comprehensive validation to ensure
the suitability and accuracy of using surrogate models for metamaterial
design and property predictions. Properly addressing these limitations
will ultimately lead to more effective and reliable metamaterial design
methodologies.
Thermal
cloak illustrates the phenomenon where the heat flux is prevented
from entering the cloaked region. In contrast, thermal transparency,
also a result of transformation heat conduction, signifies that the
heat flux can infiltrate the device without any distortion in the
heat flow, maintaining its motion as if the device were not present
in that location. Machine learning algorithms can also design thermal
transparency. Liu et al. have introduced two machine learning methods
to achieve thermal transparency in the periodic interparticle system.240,241 The device region contains circular particles marked as A and elliptical
particles marked as B with an equal number, as shown in Figure 24. Particle A has
anisotropic thermal conductivities, while B type particles have isotropic
thermal conductivities. The positions of particle A and B, as well
as their thermal conductivities, are design parameters. By means of
feed-forward neural network240 and reinforcement
learning,241 the relative positions of
circular and elliptical particles as well as the conductivities of
these particles are varied to manipulate the temperature distribution.
A baseline near the center of the device is discretized into 400 equal
distance points, and the thermal fluxes at these points are evaluated
to characterize the transparency performance. Herein, the output of
the machine learning model is a 400-dimensional vector. Thermal transparency
is defined as the thermal conductivity of composite materials or structures
equal to the backgrounds. If the device is optimized to achieve perfect
thermal transparency, one would observe the same value of heat fluxes
on all 400 points on the baseline equal to the background, as if the
periodic interparticle system is not present here. For example, if
the same thermal transparency with heat fluxes JS = 100 Wm–2 were achieved, then all 400
points on the baseline would show JS =
100 Wm–2.

(a) The autoencoder-based architecture to achieve
dimensionality
reduction for design space and response space. (b) The reinforcement
learning workflow. (c) Periodic composite material.
The first machine learning model they have chosen
is the autoencoder
based on the feed-forward neural network.240 The basic idea of their autoencoder-based model is to reduce the
dimensionality of both the original design space and the original
response space, as shown in Figure 24a. The reduced design and response space are all extracted
from the bottleneck layer at the autoencoder. Then, a third neural
network is trained using the reduced response space as input and reduced
design vectors as output. Finally, the reduced design vectors are
recovered back to the original design space by searching over the
input sets that would be reduced to give the identical reduced design
vectors. Under a given heat flux 100 Wm–2, it is
noticed that the heat fluxes at the baseline are around the prescribed
value, indicating a perfect transparency performance. Besides, the
white lines represent isotherms behaving in straight lines as if the
device does not disturb the heat flux through the entire space, intuitive
evidence of thermal transparency.
The second machine learning
method they have proved successful
in designing thermal transparency is reinforcement learning,241 as shown in Figure 24b. The FEM simulation is used to emulate
the real physics world interacting with the intelligent agent. At
each iteration step, the agent “observes” its surrounding
environment and takes action to maximize the reward value. The action
is defined as increasing or decreasing the selected parameters by
a stride. After the action is completed, the updated design parameters
are fed to the FEM environment, and a response vector that describes
the heat fluxes values of each point at the baseline is calculated.
The response vector is used to compute the reward value by comparing
the difference between the ideal and simulated transparency. Once
the training is completed, the agent can adequately help to search
for the global optimal design parameters of thermal transparency.
To guarantee that the agent can obtain a fully picture of the environment,
the observation vector should cover both the design space and the
response space. However, a 400-dimensional response vector is too
redundant and would retard the training procedure. Thus, taking use
of the autoencoder proposed in their above work, the dimensionality
of the response vector can be reduced to a 10-dimensional vector.
Contrasted with the autoencoder-driven training, which necessitates
approximately 50 000 Finite Element Method simulations, the
RL-based approach demonstrates an appreciable reduction in computational
cost. This approach only requires an initial phase encompassing 1000
FEM samples, and several thousand simulations in the fine-tuning phase.
An additional merit of the RL-based strategy lies in its extensibility,
solving the inverse design problems accompanied by constraints, and
its applicability to other thermal metamaterial devices such as cloaks.
Despite these strengths, one of the limitations of the RL-based approach
is the random generation of initial design parameters for the first
iterations, a process that could potentially be substituted with a
more intelligent initiation scheme. Such an optimized scheme could
reduce the number of episodes and mitigate the likelihood of the agent
being stuck within local minima regions.
An appropriately defined
reward function holds significant potential
to enhance the training efficiency of reinforcement learning, aligning
with the hypothesis put forth by Silver et al.242 claiming that “Reward-is-Enough”. According
to this hypothesis, once a reward function is suitably formulated,
the agent can attain human-level intelligence or even surpass it by
engaging with its environment to maximize the obtained rewards. Consequently,
the reinforcement learning based approach showcases a closer resemblance
to the nature of human intelligence, characterized by learning from
interactions and outcomes, while the supervised learning approach
exhibits a more mechanistic and rigid nature, relying solely on labeled
data for training.
A thermal
camouflage device possesses the capability to render a hot object
visually indistinguishable from the background temperature, creating
the illusion of being as cold as the surroundings. In the study conducted
by Jiang et al.,243 a multilayer film structure
was optimized for infrared camouflage by employing the Genetic Algorithm
(see Figure 25a).
The GA is initialized with 1000 individuals, each of them is encoded
with eight materials (five transparent materials in the infrared band
including SiO2, Ge, ZnS, Si, and Ge2Sb2Te5, and three metals Au, Pt, and Ag) the thicknesses
of eight layers (see Figure 25b). Interestingly, the optimization process resulted in the
merging and repetition of certain layers, leading to a reduced number
of layers in the final design. This alteration in the design simplified
the fabrication during the electron beam evaporation deposition process.
When heated at 45 °C and 60 °C, the proposed device exhibit
observed temperature 25 °C and 31.7 °C, respectively (see Figure 25d,e). The observed
temperatures clearly indicated that they were below the heating temperatures,
effectively illustrating the thermal camouflage performance of the
proposed device.

When implementing machine learning for metamaterials
design, a
crucial aspect is to select the appropriate model with high prediction
accuracy and design efficiency. As there are a variety of potential
candidate models, researchers may be unsure about the applicability
of their intended ML approach to achieving the design goal. To select
a feasible model, empirical studies and thorough literature reviews
can save considerable time in the trial-and-error process of exploring
different algorithms. As a data-driven approach, machine learning
requires representative training samples covering a wide range of
parameter space. The quality and quantity of the database significantly
influence the training accuracy. However, preparing such a data set
may prove challenging and laborious for specific problems. The lack
of a comprehensive database has posed a significant obstacle to implementing
machine learning algorithms in metamaterials design and optimization.
To address this issue, it is highly recommended to construct multiple
metamaterial databases covering as vast fields as possible for the
future development of material science.
It is envisaged that
diverse research groups within the scientific
community should engage in collaborative endeavors, facilitating the
sharing of their individual experimental and computational databases.
Through the establishment of an ample collection of databases, researchers
are afforded the opportunity to embark upon preliminary investigations.
They can apply their chosen machine learning algorithms to analogous
metamaterials databases that are pertinent to the specific problems
under investigation. This preparatory phase, involving the exploration
of relevant databases prior to full-scale research, can yield considerable
time and resource savings, ultimately contributing to enhanced research
efficiency and more fruitful outcomes. However, it is noteworthy mentioning
that the available material data might exhibit substantial interrelations.
Therefore, the preprocessing of these high-dimensional databases through
dimensionality reduction techniques becomes a necessary step prior
to the construction of descriptors.
The exploration and controllability of thermal conductivity is
essential for various applications such as thermal dissipation, heat-electricity
conversion (thermoelectrics),244 and thermal
insulation.245 When the length scales of
materials are reduced to the nanoscale, phonon transport becomes more
ballistic (or quasiballistic), and the interfacial thermal conductance
becomes a crucial factor in determining the overall thermal conduction
of the material.246,247 Phonons, as quasiparticles,
are the main heat carriers in semiconductors and dielectrics, representing
the collective vibrational modes of materials. The manipulation of
phonon behavior has emerged as a promising field to tailor thermal
properties. The thermal conductivity, under the single-mode relaxation
time approximation, can be expressed based on the phonon Boltzmann
transport equation as follows:
where n is the dispersion
branch index, k is the phonon wave vector, T is the temperature, C is the phonon specific
heat of each mode, vg is the group velocity,
and τ is the phonon lifetime. The group velocity vg = ∂ω/∂k is defined as the derivative of phonon dispersion. From the above
equation, it is quite obvious that there are several ways to change
thermal conductivity: change phonon’s lifetime τ, or
mean free path l = vgτ, and/or change group velocity vg.
The former can be done via introduction of impurity,
isotope doping or rough surface, etc., to induce additional phonon
scattering. The later, group velocity, can be modified by the design
of nanostructure. Among many others, nanophononic crystals have garnered
significant interest due to the existence of a band gap in which the
phonons cannot propagate. Nanophononic crystals are artificial periodic
structures with a periodicity of the order of the phonon wavelength.
They can exist in various dimensions, including one-dimensional (1D)
superlattices (where periodic changes in material properties occur
in a single direction),248 two-dimensional
(2D) nanomeshes,249 and three-dimensional
(3D) structures.250
The transport
of phonons depends highly on three main length scales:
the periodicity of the phononic crystal (d), the
phonon wavelength (λ), and the phonon mean free path (L̅). Phonon transport can be classified into three
regimes depending on the magnitude comparison of these three quantities:
if the periodicity of phononic crystal is smaller than the phonon
wavelength (d < λ), then phonon interference
is dominant, which is similar to wave induced by coherent scattering;
if the periodicity is larger than the phonon mean free path (d>L̅), then phonons behave like
particles and diffusive scattering effect is dominant; if the periodicity
is larger than phonon wavelength while smaller than the mean free
path (λ<d<L̅), then the scenario
is more complex which is still under debate.
Nanophononic
crystals, artificial periodic structures with periodicity comparable
to the phonon wavelength,251 offer promising
avenues for manipulating heat conduction through interface design.
However, the computational cost of searching for specific structures
with desired thermal properties becomes prohibitive due to the vast
number of candidate structures.
Bayesian optimization method
is particularly useful for searching the optimal solution using only
a few numbers of data. Hu et al.252 proposed
a Bayesian optimization method to minimize coherent phonon heat conduction
within a GaAs/AlAs aperiodic superlattice structure. The optimization
flowchart, as shown in Figure 26a, involves sampling m candidate structures
initially, and their corresponding thermal conductivities are characterized
through atomistic Green’s function calculations. These m initial candidates form the initial data set. Next, n additional structures with anticipated lower thermal conductivities
are generated using Thompson sampling. The thermal conductivities
of these n samples are characterized, and they are
then added to the initial data set. Through iterative updates of the
data set, the Bayesian optimizer effectively maps the structure–property
relationship and converges to the optimal superlattice pattern with
minimal thermal conductivity using only a small amount of data. The
optimal global structure is subsequently synthesized via molecular
beam epitaxy (MBE), and its thermal conductivity is measured using
the time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) technique across temperatures
ranging from 77 to 300 K (see Figure 26b).

(a) Flowchart of minimizing the coherent phonon heat conduction
by using Bayesian optimization as a surrogate model and characterized
by first-principles (FP) atomistic Green’s function (AGF) calculation.
(b) The global optimal aperiodic structure GaAs/AlAs. Red and gray
layers denote GaAs (0) and AlAs (1), respectively. (c) Reference periodic
structure. (d) Experimental and simulated thermal conductivities of
the optimized aperiodic and periodic structures for a temperature
range from 50 to 300 K. The smooth curves are simulation results of
ideal structures, while dashed curves have considered the interfacial
roughness between GaAs and AlAs layers. Optimized thermal conductivity
of the aperiodic SLs (blue) is always smaller than that of the periodic
SLs (red) throughout the temperature range. (e) Weighted inverse participation
ratio (IPR) as a function of acoustic phonon frequency, and larger
weighted IPR values demonstrate the phonons are highly localized.

A periodic counterpart is also fabricated for comparison
with the
machine learning optimized structure (see Figure 26c). As depicted in Figure 26d, the thermal conductivity of the optimized
aperiodic structure remains consistently lower than that of the periodic
reference over the entire temperature range. The labels “smooth”
and “rough” represent the ideal and imperfect superlattice
sample, respectively. The roughness arises from the experimental error
between GaAs and AlAs interface, which involves: (i) the fabricated
structure is one atom layer short in the thick AlAs layers, and (ii)
monolayer roughness at the interfaces can occur due to the interdiffusion
between Ga and Al atoms. The reduced thermal conductivity is attributed
to the significant localization of acoustic phonons that hinder heat
transport, evident in the stronger peaks of the weighted inverse participation
ratio (see Figure 26e), and the transmission of phonons are inhibited by the optimal
local structures among a wide frequency range.
In addition to
optimizing thermal conductance for the overall material,
tuning the interfacial thermal conductance (ITC) between two ends
is another important aspect of thermal materials. Ju et al.253 have also introduced Bayesian optimization
to maximize and minimize the ITC by tuning the Si/Ge composite between
the Si–Si interface (Si is located at two ends) or Si–Ge
interface (Si is at one end while Ge is at the opposite end), as shown
in Figure 27a. The
descriptor is also composed of two text indexes with “1”
and “0” indicating the Ge and Si atoms, respectively.
The atomistic Green’s function is used to characterize the
ITC of the generated structures. The optimization process can all
converge after evaluating only 3.4% of the total possible structure
candidates, and the ratios of the maximum to minimum ITC between the
Si–Si or Si–Ge interfaces are 2.4 and 2.2, respectively.
They have proved that the reduced thermal conductance originates from
two competing effects: Fabry–Perot wave interference and interfacial
particle scattering, which further cause the suppression of constructive
phonon interference by aperiodic structure.

Bayesian optimization as a surrogate model
to maximize and minimize the interfacial thermal conductivities (ITC)
between Si–Si and Si–Ge interfaces. (b) Optimal structures
with the maximum and minimum ITC for Si–Si and Si–Ge
interface with different sizes of supercell cross section (1 UC ×

Chowdhury et al.254 conducted
a study
to identify the Si/Ge random multilayer nanostructure that exhibits
the globally minimum thermal conductivity. To achieve this, they employed
a combination of a genetic algorithm search process and nonequilibrium
molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulations. In their approach, they used
a binary array of N bits to encode the random multilayer
structure, where N represents the length of the structure
in the cross-plane direction. This binary array served as the chromosomes,
as depicted in Figure 28a. Each position in the chromosome was assigned a value of 1 if it
corresponded to a Si unit cell and 2 if it corresponded to a Ge unit
cell. To explore various combinations effectively, the genetic algorithm
applied crossover to selected individuals, generating two new offspring.
Additionally, probabilistic mutation was employed by flipping the
gene string between 1 and 2 to further diversify the population. The
researchers conducted 15 independent runs, and it was observed that
the lowest conductivity value reached a saturation point after 35
generations. Convergence of the search process was achieved when the
lowest thermal conductivity value remained constant over several successive
iterations, as shown in Figure 28b. The globally optimal structure with the minimum
thermal conductivity was identified and depicted in Figure 28c. This optimization method
can be applied broadly to other systems, such as graphene sheets with
disordered arrangements of pores or superlattices with rough interfaces
formed by different geometries.

Schematic of the genetic algorithm optimization
method searching
for globally optimal minimum thermal conductivity of Si/Ge aperiodic
superlattice, characterized by NEMD simulations. (b) Evolution of
thermal conductivity of one run in genetic algorithm search process.
(c) Random multilayer structure with minimum thermal conductivity
obtained from 15 individual runs. Reproduced with permission from
ref (254). Copyright
2020 Elsevier.
It is observed that, in the case of a multilayer
structure, the
descriptor used to encode the superlattice exhibits relative simplicity.
For example, if each layer possesses uniform thickness, the descriptor
takes the form of a vector comprised of numerical values, often denoted
as “1” and “2,” corresponding to different
materials. This straightforward yet practical descriptor underscores
the principle that the design of a descriptor need not always be overly
complex, incorporating an excessive number of variables. A guiding
principle for constructing a material representation can be paraphrased
from Occam’s razor, a notion often attributed to Einstein,
emphasizing that a descriptor should be “as simple as possible,
but not simpler.” The optimal performance of learning algorithms
is achieved only when essential variables are effectively encoded
within the descriptor. Therefore, an improvement in the performance
of machine learning models is not guaranteed by the inclusion of an
abundance of variables (such as chemical compositions or stoichiometry)
beyond the key factors. To develop a systematic, physically grounded,
and computationally efficient material representation, certain universal
prerequisites have been proposed in the literature.255,256 These requirements can be summarized into two primary aspects. First,
uniqueness and distinctiveness: two materials share an identical descriptor
only when they are fundamentally the same, while distinct materials
should be discernible through distinct representations. Second, efficiency
and simplicity: the representation encompasses essential information,
enabling swift computational processing.
The abnormal thermal
conductivity enhancement in superlattice structures
presents an enticing area for exploration. However, manual search
methods suffer from unreliability due to the vast design space of
superlattice configurations and the high failure rate when relying
solely on human intelligence. To address this challenge, Chowdhury
et al.257 utilized a Convolutional Neural
Network (CNN)-based active learning method to discover an unexpected
enhancement in thermal conductivities in Si/Ge aperiodic superlattice
structures when compared with their periodic counterparts. In their
study, an N-bit array was employed, with each bit taking a value of
1 or 2 to represent the unit cell (UC) material of Si or Ge atoms
at specific locations in the superlattice (see Figure 29a). The number of candidate multilayer structures
for 20 UC and 40 UC are 48,620 and 35,345,263,800, respectively. The
CNN was initially trained on a data set of 300 randomly generated
superlattice structures and was then used to predict another 100 potential
candidates with promisingly enhanced thermal conductivities (denoted
as kCNN). These predictions were subsequently
verified by using nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations (denoted
as kNEMD). If the thermal conductivities
of the 100 candidate structures were not enhanced, they were included
in the training data set to retrain the CNN. If any of the 100 structures
exhibit a higher thermal conductivity (κNEMD) than the periodic structure, the search process is stopped.
This process allowed the trained CNN to predict the thermal conductivities
of all structures in the search space, eventually leading to the discovery
of the optimal structure with the highest thermal conductivity (see Figure 29b). Notably, the
CNN exhibited accurate predictions over a wide range of thermal conductivities,
ranging from 1 to 2.5 W/mK (see Figure 29c). The neural network successfully identified
the optimal structures with enhanced thermal conductivities for both
the 20 UC and 40 UC systems (see Figure 29d). Importantly, the machine learning-based
search process demonstrated efficiency, requiring only 200 CPU hours
to identify the best structure. In comparison, manual random search
demanded double the computational time while still yielding far lower
thermal conductivity values (Kl). For the respective optimized superlattices with 20- and
40-unit cells, the thermal conductivities exhibited enhancements of
3.5% and 5.5% higher than their corresponding periodic counterparts,
showcasing the potential of machine learning algorithms in optimizing
superlattice structures for enhanced thermal properties.

The smooth interface between Si and Ge can be further
modified
by incorporating multiple interfacial nanostructures, and numerous
studies have highlighted that interfacial nanostructuring represents
an effective approach to manipulate interfacial thermal conductance.258−260 Interfacial thermal transport is significantly influenced by various
geometrical variables of nanostructures, such as height, contact angle,
and density. Consequently, the optimization through nanostructuring
has emerged as an ongoing and appealing area of research. Jin et al.261 have demonstrated the application of random
forest regression in accurately predicting the thermal resistance
between Si/Ge heterostructures, following a training process with
an input descriptor comprising three structural parameters: h, θ, and d, as depicted in Figure 30. The well-trained
random forest model effectively substitutes the need for molecular
dynamics simulations to investigate the impact of geometrical parameters
on interfacial thermal resistance. The insights gained from the machine
learning-based model shed light on the dependence of interfacial thermal
resistance on nanostructuring, offering comprehensive guidance for
optimizing thermal transport in such systems.

(a) The Si/Ge heterostructure
with heat source and heat sink at
two ends. The interfacial nanostructures, i.e., nanocones, are described
by three structural parameters including distance between nanocones
(d), height of nanocones (h), and
angle of nanocones (θ). (b) The machine learning predicted thermal
resistance Rpred versus simulated thermal
resistance value Rsim. Reproduced with

Graphene has gained
immense interest over the past decade due to its exceptional physical
properties. However, pristine graphene’s lack of a bandgap
limits its applications in semiconducting devices.262 To address this limitation, recent experiments have introduced
controllable nanoscale holes in graphene to open a finite bandgap
and significantly reduce its thermal conductivity.263 The reduction of thermal conductivity has great potential
for various applications, especially in thermoelectric materials and
devices. Nonetheless, determining the optimal distribution of these
holes to minimize thermal conductivity remains a challenging question,
primarily because the design space expands exponentially with an increasing
number of holes. To tackle this inverse design challenge, Wan et al.264 have proposed a novel approach based on CNN
after establishing the relationship between hole distribution and
thermal conductivity in monolayer graphene. Each training data point
is represented as a gray image of size 54 × 50, and its corresponding
thermal conductivity is characterized through molecular dynamics (MD)
simulations. Inspired by the classic CNN model VGGNet, the researchers
have designed their own optimal CNN architecture, denoted as CNN-c16c32c64f64,
featuring 16 kernels in the first convolutional layer, 32 kernels
in the second convolutional layer, 64 kernels in the third convolutional
layer, and 64 neurons in the fully connected layer. The CNN architecture
demonstrates a high regression performance, with R2 values close to 1 in both the training, validation,
and test sets, effectively minimizing the risk of overfitting. The
researchers initially randomly selected 100 structures from the entire
library of possible structures and calculated their thermal conductivities
using MD simulations, as the training data, which was utilized to
train the first-generation CNN model. Subsequently, the model was
used to predict the thermal conductivity of all the remaining structures
in the library. By identifying the 100 structures with the lowest
predicted thermal conductivity, their corresponding true thermal conductivity
values were computed through further MD simulations. The data obtained
for these 100 newly predicted structures were then incorporated into
the training set, expanding its size as the design process iteratively
progresses, as illustrated in Figure 31b. The CNN-based model has successfully identified
porous structures with the lowest thermal conductivities, as is demonstrated
in Figure 31c. This
approach presents a promising strategy for the inverse design of porous
metamaterial structures with minimized thermal properties.

(a) The structure
of porous graphene. Atom clusters (blue outline)
in the middle region are candidate sites for creating holes. (b) Schematic
of workflow searching for minimum thermal conductivity based on the
CNN model. (c) The porous structure of the top 5 configurations with
lowest thermal conductivities discovered by CNN model. Reproduced
with permission from ref (264). Copyright 2020 Elsevier.
The remarkable capabilities of machine learning
have the potential
to assist scientists in uncovering counterintuitive and unconventional
phenomena, thereby serving as a significant pathway to make evolutionary
breakthroughs in scientific theories and deepen our understanding
of physics. In porous metamaterials, the introduction of pores typically
leads to a reduction in thermal conductivity.265 By leveraging machine learning, an optimal distribution
of pores that achieves the minimized thermal conductivity can be identified,
as demonstrated in Figure 31. However, it is noteworthy that the machine learning approach
can also reveal an unexpected and counterintuitive outcome, wherein
an appropriate distribution of pores actually maximizes the thermal
conductivity of metamaterials. This counterintuitive phenomenon, discovered
through machine learning, challenges conventional assumptions and
offers new insights into metamaterials.
Yang et al.266 have demonstrated that
effective thermal conductivity can be abnormally enhanced by approximately
7.9% or normally reduced by approximately 44% through the introduction
of suitable disordered pores, employing a multilayer perception (MLP)
combined with the particle swarm optimization algorithm. Initially,
an ordered two-dimensional porous alumina sheet comprised periodic
pores uniformly arranged along the x and y directions (see Figure 32a). To create a data set for training, the position
of each pore was randomly perturbed, generating multiple disordered
configurations. As shown in Figure 32b, the jth pore is disturbed by the
displacements δj,x and δj,y along x and y direction. The effective thermal conductivity κe is calculated by the finite element method (FEM) with
Fourier’s law κe = J/ΔT. Here J is the average thermal flux of
the entire porous material under external temperature difference ΔT. The prediction ability for effective thermal conductivity
of MLP is reflected by the high correlation coefficient R = 0.9856 and the very small mean square error, MSE = 1.9 ×
10–4 (see Figure 32d,e). The PSO algorithm starts with a swarm of 300
design configurations (particles), each configuration containing a
32-dimensional parameter space. All configurations will search the
parameter space to generate the next generation. During the evolution
process, each particle will remember its personal best solution and
global best solution within the entire population. These memories
serve as attractors in the parameter space and drive the particles
to converge to the global best design solutions. Notably, the researchers
experimentally realized the optimal configuration and successfully
validated the theoretically optimized abnormal enhancement and normal
reduction of thermal conductivity (see Figure 32f).

Temperature distribution and partial
thermal flux line (brown curve)
of the periodically arranged configuration. (b) An illustration of
moving the pore to construct the disordered configuration. (c) The
flowchart of PSO algorithm. (d) The MSE of the training set and validation
set during the training step. (e) The accuracy of effective thermal
conductivity obtained by comparing the prediction of trained MLP and
the finite element method (FEM) verification. (f) The experimental
measurement results of the effective thermal conductivity of the largest
(red diamond), uniform arrangement configuration (green circle), and
smallest configuration (blue square) under different temperature differences.

Wei et al.267 also made
a notable discovery
of unexpected thermal conductivity enhancement in nanoporous graphene
with the aid of the genetic algorithm. As shown in Figure 33a, the period L0 and porosity were held constant, while the pores were
randomly shifted to nearby positions to introduce disorder effects.
To reduce the search space and computational complexity, the optimization
process was initially conducted with a reduced-size configuration
containing 16 pores. The corresponding large-size configuration was
then constructed by replicating the small-size optimal pattern along
the x or y direction (see Figure 33b). The convergence
criterion for the genetic algorithm was set such that the thermal
conductivity of the best individual in each generation remained unchanged
for eight consecutive generations (see Figure 33c). Starting from a periodic configuration
with normalized thermal conductivity of 3.97 × 10–3, they have obtained optimal patterns with normalized thermal conductivities
of 4.27 × 10–3 and 4.35 × 10–3 in x and y directions, which are
approximately 8% and 10% higher than that of the periodic configuration,
respectively (see Figure 33d). Notably, the computational time required for the genetic
algorithm was only 6604 core hours, which accounted for merely 10%
of the time cost incurred by manual search (67 200 core hours).
Furthermore, despite an extensive amount of searching time, the manual
search failed to produce a disorder-enhanced case. This discovery
underscores the effectiveness of machine learning in exploring and
uncovering small probability events, showcasing its potential in investigating
unconventional phenomena with improved efficiency and accuracy. In
addition to the manipulation of pores’ distribution, Yang et
al.268 have optimized the mass distribution
of 1D atomic chain with Bayesian optimization to achieve the maximum
and minimum interfacial thermal conductance.

Thermal
radiation is a ubiquitous phenomenon in nature. Any objects that are
at nonzero temperatures emit electromagnetic energy. The emission
of thermal energy from an object at temperature T can be characterized by its spectral radiance Ll (θ,ϕ,ν,T), defined as the emitted power per unit solid angle (θ,ϕ),
per unit frequency at ν, per unit area, in polarization state l. Expression of the spectral radiance of a blackbody LBB (ν,T) is described by the Planck’ law:
where c is the speed of light, h is Planck’s constant, and kB is the Boltzmann constant. The spectral radiance of a blackbody
is independent of angle and polarization state. Equation 22 describes the scenario where a blackbody
in thermal equilibrium with a surrounding photon reservoir in free
space, and its emitted energy density matches the energy density of
the reservoir. According to the Bose–Einstein statistics, the
expected number of photons in a specific electromagnetic mode at frequency v is . Integrating the equation over all frequencies
and angles gives rise to the Stefan–Boltzmann law, which relates
the total irradiance I of a blackbody to its temperature:
In practice, the thermal emission spectrum
of a real object deviates from that of an ideal blackbody. In the
far field regime at temperature T, the thermal emissivity
εl(ν, θ, ϕ, T)
is defined as the ratio of spectral radiance of thermal emission from
an object to that of an ideal blackbody:
For a blackbody, εl(ν,
θ, ϕ, T) = Al(ν, θ, ϕ, T) = 1, where Al(ν, θ, ϕ, T) denotes the
absorptivity. According to the Kirchhoff’s law of thermal radiation,269 the emissivity and absorptivity are equivalent:
εl(ν, θ, ϕ, T)
= Al(ν, θ,
ϕ, T).
When the distance of objects with thermal radiation
is larger than
the thermal wavelength, the radiation is in the far-field regime.201 Studies on manipulating far-field radiation
have been prolific recently because it plays a pivotal role in solar
energy harvesting and radiative cooling. When the distance between
objects with radiative heat transfer becomes subwavelength, the amount
of transferred heat is enhanced and exceeds the case of the far-field
case,270 rendering a new application at
the microscale. The near-field enhancement effect can be understood
by a simple physics scenario. Consider two identical semi-infinite
mediums whose temperatures are T1 and T2(T1 > T2), and they are separated by a vacuum of width d, then the radiative heat flux per unit area q across the gap is expressed as:271
where Θ(ω,T1,2) = ℏω/[exp(ℏω/kBT) – 1] and k is the wave vector. ξs (ω,k) and ξp (ω,k) quantify the photon
transmission probabilities for the transverse electric (s) and transverse
magnetic (p) polarizations, respectively. For propagating waves, they
can be expressed as:
And for evanescent waves:
where r1,2 quantify
the Fresnel reflection coefficients for incident wave from the wave
to medium 1 and 2, k0 = ω/c is the free-space wavenumber and kz0 is the out-of-plane wavenumber
in vacuum. Both ξs and ξp are within
the region [0,1]. In the far-field case, only the propagating waves
contribute to the total heat flux. While for the near-field regime,
the evanescent wave become more evident and contributes to the total
heat radiation due to the increased term e–2|kz0|d at the numerator as d is reduced. Including
the evanescent contribution makes the heat flux density in the near-field
regime exceed that in the far-field regime by order of magnitude.
Thermal radiation is a pervasive phenomenon, with all materials emitting
and absorbing thermal energy. However, a substantial amount of thermal
energy, such as losses from semiconductor equipment, goes to waste
and is dissipated into the environment.272,273 It is crucial to address this issue by recycling wasted energy to
enhance energy utilization efficiency and promote environmentally
friendly practices. The development of thermophotovoltaic (TPV) systems
offers a promising solution to mitigate global warming. In a solar
thermophotovoltaic (STPV) device, photons are radiated from thermal
emitters then absorbed by photovoltaic (PV) cells and converted into
electricity by the photoelectric effect.274,275
In solar energy harvesting, the conventional photovoltaic
technique faces several limitations that significantly reduce its
efficiency, keeping it well below the Carnot efficiency limit of ∼95%.
For a single-junction PV, it can only absorb photons with energy above
the bandgap, leading to the loss of the difference between photon
energy and the bandgap as heat. These losses, along with losses from
radiative recombination, primarily contribute to the theoretical efficiency
limitations of photovoltaic systems for nonconcentrated sunlight.
For instance, the Shockley–Queisser limit sets the theoretical
efficiency at approximately 33% for single-junction cells, ∼42%
for two-junction cells, and ∼49% for three-junction cells.276
TPV systems offer a promising approach
to surpassing the Shockley–Queisser
limit. In the TPV system, an intermediate element is optimized to
generate large thermal emissivity and narrow bandwidth after absorbing
the incident sunlight.277 The intermediate
element is mainly composed of a thermal absorber and emitter. The
solar photons are initially absorbed by a broadband absorber, leading
to a rise in its temperature. Subsequently, the energy is transferred
to a photovoltaic (PV) cell through a frequency-selective thermal
emitter278 (see Figure 34a).

(a) Schematic of a solar thermophotovoltaic
(TPV) device composed
of a broadband solar absorber, a selective thermal emitter, and a
PV cell. (b) A vast amount of solar energy consists of photons with
energies below the typical photovoltaic (PV) bandgap is not absorbed
by the PV cell. A solar TPV device facilitates the solar energy to
be converted to photons right above the PV bandgap via a selective
thermal emitter. Reproduced with permission from ref (276). Copyright 2019 Springer.
The ideal solar absorber is designed to capture
energy from a broad
spectrum, encompassing ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared regions.
Simultaneously, it should suppress thermal radiation in the mid-infrared
range to minimize energy loss to the ambient environment. The reason
for this design is that only the in-band radiation is responsible
for producing electron–hole pairs, while the out-of-band radiation
causes undesirable heating of the PV cell, leading to a significant
reduction in its quantum efficiency and device lifetime. Thus, it
is highly desirable to maximize in-band radiation while minimizing
out-of-band radiation to optimize TPV system performance. However,
achieving high absorption within a broad wavelength range using naturally
existing materials is challenging, as most materials exhibit specific
absorption peaks due to their intrinsic electronic and atomic structures.279 The ideal thermal emitter should possess a
narrow emissivity peak, slightly above the bandgap of the PV cell,
to maximize the conversion efficiency at the cell element280 (see Figure 34b). In other words, the optimal thermal emitter should
have high thermal emissivity at the target wavelength region with ε(λmin < λ < λmax) ≈ 1 and zero elsewhere, with narrow-band and high
Q factor. Additionally, because TPV systems operate at high temperatures,
the thermal emitter must be designed by using high-temperature stable
material. Recent advances in metamaterials and nanophononics research
have made various nanostructures, such as multilayers,281 metasurfaces,282 photonic crystals,283 and Tamm plasmons,284 promising candidates for TPV system enhancement.
The multilayer structure offers superior advantages due to its
scalable manufacturing and adjustable performance. Additionally, its
structure is more straightforward to code into a descriptor, represented
as a 1D vector. As a result, many studies have employed machine learning
algorithms to optimize the multilayer structure in TPV systems. The
thermal emission of the multilayer structure can be calculated using
the transfer matrix method (TMM). In TMM, the optical response of
each layer (labeled as l = 1,2, . . .,N) is described by its relative permittivity.285 The optical responses of different layers are connected
through a transfer matrix, as follows:

To calculate the system efficiency,
we need to consider the energy
balance analysis. The incident photon energy from the emitter is:

where ηquantum is the wavelength-dependent quantum efficiency of the PV cell. The
factor λ/λbg demonstrates that only photons
with energy greater than the bandgap energy can generate photocurrent.
The usable power of the PV cell can be calculated as the difference
between the absorbed photon energy and the nonradiative energy loss
as Puse = Pabs – Ploss = Pabs – eVR, and the power density P of the PV cell is P = JV. Finally, the system efficiency is η = Puse/Pin. A higher power density P is important to minimize the efficiency loss in PV cell
due to the loss of open-circuit voltage, and a large η is also
significant to minimize the thermalization loss.
Among various
metamaterial structures used for thermal emitters, multilayers hold
advantages over other thermal radiators due to their ease of nanofabrication
and scalability. However, in practice, the prevalent designs are often
periodic structures.286−288 The aperiodic multilayers have been relatively
less explored due to the enormous number of possible candidates in
the search space.289,290 To address this challenge, a
reverse approach using machine learning discriminative models to directly
generate metamaterial structures by inputting the desired response
has been proposed by So et al.291 recently.
They trained an artificial neural network (ANN) using emissivity spectra
as input and design variables as output for the inverse design task.
The total data set of 243 675 samples was divided into three
subsets: 80% for training, 10% for validation, and 10% for testing.
Each input vector consisted of 300 equidistant spectral points covering
the wavelength regime of 2–8 μm on the emissivity spectra.
The design variables are the section of the material (Mat, including
Si, Ge, and Si3N4) and its thickness (tMat), the thickness of the SiO2 (tSiO2), and the thickness of the Si
layer (tSi), as shown in Figure 35a. Thus, output vector is Y = [Y1,Y2,Y3,Y4,Y5,Y6 ]
= [p(Si),p(Ge),p(Si3N4),tSi,t(SiO2),tMat]. The
choice of material is a classification problem that ANN is trained
to produce a one-hot vector ([Y1,Y2,Y3]), then selecting
the highest probability p. In contrast, the prediction
of thicknesses of the layers is a regression problem and ANN is trained
to minimize the mean square error (MSE, lthickness loss). After 5000 training, the ANN converged with a loss around 0.06.
As shown in Figure 35b, when a test spectrum was input to the ANN, the design parameters
were predicted, and the design proposal was verified using rigorous
coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD)
simulations. The examples demonstrated excellent agreement between
the test and designed emissivity spectra obtained from RCWA and FDTD.
The researchers successfully achieved the inverse design task by using
Lorentzian-like functions as target input emissivity spectra at different
peak wavelengths. The trained ANN produced corresponding design parameters
that generated spectra in good agreement with the design requirements
(see Figure 35c–h).
The design space only incorporates four design parameters, and this
method could be easily expanded to a larger design parameter space.

architecture of the ANN. (b) Examples of the test results. The solid

are designed emissivity spectra obtained from RCWA and FDTD simulations,

However, it should be noted that directly reversing
the discriminative
model to output the design space may lead to nonuniqueness solutions.
For instance, the researchers reported that two materials were able
to produce high-Q emitters with similar targeted emissivity spectra
(see Figure 35c,d).
The nonuniqueness can make neural networks unable to converge.292 To overcome this problem, probabilistic models
such as the variational autoencoder could be employed. Yet machine
learning in optimization and inverse design of thermal metamaterials
is still in its early stages, generative models have not yet been
extensively incorporated in this field. Further research and exploration
in this direction are required.
Bayesian optimization293 offers a systematic
approach for efficiently navigating the design space and pinpointing
optimal solutions. A notable application of Bayesian optimization
is demonstrated by Sakurai et al.294 who
leveraged this technique to design an optimal ultranarrow wavelength-selective
thermal emitter tailored to targeted wavelengths, as illustrated in Figure 36. The metamaterial
is divided into N (N = 18) layers
with varying thicknesses dt; each unit layer is assigned
one of the materials from potential candidates Ge, Si, and SiO2, with the substrate material fixed as tungsten (see Figure 36a). A descriptor
used is defined as a set of number indexes “1”, “2”,
and “3” representing Ge, Si, and SiO2 to
describe the selected material for each layer as a possible structure
pattern. The emissivity spectrum for one structure pattern is calculated
by the transfer matrix method (TMM). Given three targeted wavelengths
of 5.0, 6.0, and 7.0 μm, the optimizer can produce the optimal
aperiodic structure with the material and thickness for each layer.
It is highlighted that the emissivities of these radiators are unity
(see Figure 36b),
and their Q-factors are 217, 273, and 233, respectively. The nominated
structures are fabricated by sputtering and the measured peak emissivity
values are 0.76, 0.83, and 0.61 (see Figure 36c), and the Q-factors are 132, 188, and
109, respectively. It turns out that the enhanced thermal emissivity
is due to the strong confinements of electromagnetic energy in the
Ge layer for targeted wavelengths at 5.0 and 6.0 μm, and SiO2 at 7.0 μm from the magnetic field profiles (see Figure 36d–f). Thus,
machine learning can solve the design issue and expand our understanding
of the emissivity enhancement mechanism. Compared with the machine
learning algorithms reported in other literature, the Bayesian optimization
method shows significantly improved efficacy as it can explore the
optimal global solution by using only 2.06% of the candidate structures.

As shown in Figure 37a, Zhang et al.295 have also used Bayesian
optimization to design an aperiodic thermal radiator using either
W, Si, or SiO2 for each unit layer. In contrast, they decide
the total number of layers n = 10, and the thickness
of each layer is selected from three choices (45, 55, and 65 nm).
The optimal emitter displays the figure of merit 82.61% and 81.35%
for simulation and experimental measurements. The slight discrepancy
between these two values is mainly caused by the thickness error of
each layer during multitarget sputtering processing, which changes
the corresponding optical properties. Besides, nanostructures may
form at the interface between layers with different materials, further
affecting the emission spectrum by reducing the applicability of the
transfer matrix method. Bayesian optimization has also saved the calculation
resource as it only utilizes less than 0.67% of the total candidate
structures. The Si layer and W layer contribute the most to improved
emissivity due to a strong magnetic field enhancement in the Si layer
and W layer interface (see Figure 37d,e).

Bayesian optimization method can be further combined
with generative
networks. Zhu et al.296 synergistically
integrates the capabilities of the adversarial autoencoder and Bayesian
optimization techniques for designing narrow-band thermal emitters
operating at distinct target wavelengths. The hybrid framework leverages
the strengths of both AAE and BO, capitalizing on the efficient exploration
of the design space facilitated by AAE and the precision of optimization
provided by BO. With only several hundreds of training data sets on
AAE, the optimal design is obtained by calculating far less than 0.001%
of the total candidate structures. Besides, the maximum figure of
merit of each recommended structure at different target wavelengths
from AAE+BO showcases a much larger value than that proposed from
pure Bayesian optimization approach. The hybrid optimization framework,
therefore, significantly enhances search efficiency, a characteristic
that holds potential for broader applicability across various inverse
design scenarios. Hu et al.285 have also
investigated a 1D-multilayer Tamm emitter by employing machine-learning
Monte Carlo tree search algorithm. The optimization process, in this
case, extends beyond a singular objective and considers two pivotal
figure-of-merit parameters, power density and system efficiency. The
optimization endeavor achieves an ideal emissivity spectrum, a task
rendered challenging by the inherent trade-offs between competing
objectives during the optimization procedure. Their optimization method
can be extended for the multiobjective optimization problems in other
fields. Jiang et al.297 have achieved high
emissivity ε = 0.85 of a selective thermal emitter for nonatmospheric
window 5–8 μm assisted by a direct binary algorithm.
They have employed a phase-change material Ge2Sb2Te5 (GST) as the intermediate layer within the metal–insulator–metal
structure owing to the tunability of GST. The tunability inherent
to GST allows for precise control over the thermal emission characteristics,
thus enabling the realization of a selective emitter with tunable
thermal radiation spanning the wavelength range of 3–14 μm.
Their innovative approach highlights the potential of employing advanced
material constituents to achieve tailored and controllable thermal
radiation properties for specific applications.
The nanostructures
elucidated earlier exhibit characteristic dimensions
commensurate with the wavelength of thermal radiation, a regime referred
to as far-field thermal radiation control. In contrast, the near-field
radiative heat transfer (NFRHT) pertains to scenarios where the gap
size is comparable to, or even smaller than, the thermal wavelength.
In such configurations, NFRHT transcends the confines of the far-field
blackbody limit by orders of magnitude,298−302 endowing it with significant potential to underpin the advancement
of thermophotovoltaic devices. This unique attribute of NFRHT has
engendered its application across a variety of fields, encompassing
electronic devices and renewable energy harnessing, primarily owing
to its capacity for exceedingly efficient energy transmission.303−305
In optimization of the NFRHT, Wen et al.306 have combined an artificial neural network as well as a
genetic
algorithm to obtain the optimum design parameters for the largest
radiative heat flow Qpla and rectification
ratio. Instead of using the scattering theory and effective medium
theory to calculate the energy transmission coefficient, the trained
neural network can accurately predict the heat flow in less time,
which can be used as a surrogate model to accelerate the optimization
process by applying the Genetic Algorithm. The basic device is the
two multilayered metamaterials composed of doped silicon (at different
doping concentrations Dsi) and germanium
(Ge) with varying thicknesses. Thus, the design parameters including
thickness of doped silicon and germanium tm, td, the period of a unit cell P = tm + td, the doping concentration Dsi, the distance between the two multilayered superlattice dpla can and the temperature of the two mutilayered
structure Th, Tl can be freely integrated for different combination to constitute
the input vectors (see Figure 38a). Here, they have used a two-input model [input:(tm,td),output:Qpla], a four-input model [input:(tm,td,dpla,Th),output:Qpla], and a five-input model [input:(tm, td,dpla,Th,Dsi),output:Qpla] as the input/output vectors to train
the neural network considering to obtain a better reflection of the
near-field enhancement mechanism. The low-temperature domain Tl = 0 K in all cases. The optimization time
using a surrogate can be no more than 1 min. For the four-input model,
the large contribution of transmission coefficient is mainly caused
by the excitation of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) at the interface
between Si and vacuum. As for the five-input model, it turns out that
a lower doping concentration can result in a higher value of output,
which demonstrates that the machine learning model can adjust the
resonant frequency of the excited mode when incorporating doping as
one of the input parameters. To further validate the applicability
of their approach, they have extended the workflow to optimize the
NFRHT and rectification ratio between two polytype 3D-SiC nanoparticles
(see Figure 38b).
Training with the five-input model, the error between the predicted
by the neural network surrogate model and the accurate ones for the
optimized model are no more than 1%. Furthermore, incorporating a
machine learning surrogate model with evolutionary algorithms can
be extended to other fields of metamaterial study.307,308

(a) Schematic of near-field thermal radiation between two multilayered
metamaterials. (b) Outline of proposed optimization strategy by combing
machine learning with Genetic Algorithm.
So far, we have discussed emitter structures based
on the multilayer
framework, and another type of metamaterial structure for a TPV system
is the two-dimensional grating structure. Zhao et al.309 applied the Bayesian algorithm to optimize
the infrared grating nanostructure for achieving wavelength-selective
emission. The emitter is a metal–insulator–metal nanostructure
composed of a tungsten grating on a SiO2 dielectric layer
and a tungsten substrate in sequence. Tungsten is selected as the
gratings and substrates material owing to its high thermal conductivity,
high refractory properties. The structure of the selective emitter
to be optimized is represented by the period (Γ), the filling
factor (f), the thickness of gratings (d1), and the thickness of SiO2 layer (d2), and the flowchart of the optimization process
is shown in Figure 39a. After evaluating only less than 0.173% of the total candidate
structures, the optimal emitter give rise to system efficiency and
power density as Pout = 4.2 W/cm2 and η = 35.4%, denoted as the red dot in Figure 39b, and the optimization history
is traced by the evolution of the figure of merit as shown in Figure 39c. The Bayesian
optimization algorithm efficiently guided the search process to discover
the optimal emitter design with remarkable performance improvements,
achieving both high system efficiency and power density for the TPV
system.

in the optimization process. (c) The iterative process of Bayesian
