The surface patterns of thermal emitters can be
extended to arbitrary
geometries, and the optimization of surface geometrical topology can
be achieved through machine learning generative models. Kudyshev et
al.310 have adapted the adversarial autoencoder
to improve the optimization process substantially in terms of less
computational time (4900 times faster) and high efficiency (∼98%)
of the thermal emitter with a working band range of 0.5–1.7
μm. The three-layer structure contains a back TiN reflector,
a Si3N4 spacer, and a TiN top layer, which is
defined as the optimization region and discretized into matrix elements,
as shown in Figure 40. The AAE consists of three coupled neural networks: encoder, decoder/generator,
and discriminator. The encoder compresses a given input pattern into
a compact design space, known as a latent space. Subsequently, the
decoder learns to reconstruct the actual input pattern based on a
given latent vector. The AAE performs adversarial learning, similar
to GAN, by incorporating a discriminator to force the latent space
to follow a predefined model distribution. Hence, the AAE can be viewed
as a combination of VAE and GAN. During the training process, the
encoder is trained to perform two key tasks: (i) it takes a 64 ×
64 binary, greyscale image of the top layer as input and compresses
it into a 15-dimensional vector, which represents a position in the
15-dimensional latent space used by the decoder for reconstruction,
and (ii) it generates an extra latent sampling that needs to pass
the evaluation by the discriminator to resemble a sample from the
predefined model distribution. Meanwhile, the decoder functions as
a generator that takes the latent coordinate as input and reconstructs
the design pattern in the real space. Simultaneously, the discriminator
supervises the latent space produced by the encoder to match the predefined
distribution.

AAE-assisted optimization schematics.
Upon completion of training, the decoder operates
as a generator
of new designs. The generated designs are further subjected to refinement
through a filtering process, which eliminates small and sharp features
in the designs produced by the AAE. Subsequently, a pretrained CNN
is employed to predict the efficiency of these emitters (see Figure 41a). For this purpose,
a smaller version of the VGGnet network is selected as the CNN architecture
(see Figure 41b).
The prediction performance of the trained VGGnet regression model
displays r2 = 0.93, indicating a high
accuracy. Remarkably, approximately 88% of the designs generated by
using AAE+VGGnet exhibit high efficiency levels above 80%, with the
best design achieving an impressive efficiency of 95.5%. Moreover,
the optimal generated configuration enables almost all available in-band
emission while effectively suppressing out-of-band radiation. Furthermore,
the AAE+VGGnet approach demonstrates exceptional efficiency by generating
100 highly efficient designs (>80%) within just 2 min, which is
approximately
4900 times faster than using conventional topological optimization
methods. This training process of the AAE enables efficient inverse
design and optimization of thermal emitters with complex surface patterns
and arbitrary geometries. It significantly reduces computational time
while maintaining high optimization efficiency.

(a) Structure refinement
and filtering scheme. The trained AAE
generator is used for design generation, and the proposed designs
are refined with either (i) a topological optimization based approach,
and (ii) the pretrained VGGnet filtering the high efficiency structures.
(b) Schematics of the VGGnet type network used for design efficiency
prediction and robustness classification.
The AAE network can be further extended beyond
random sampling
of designs by incorporating the geometrical parameters of the unit
cell as constraints along with the topology of the emitter’s
surface structure. This type of neural network is referred to as a
conditional adversarial autoencoder (c-AAE). The c-AAE can introduce
physics-driven regularization to compress the design space during
training, leading to improved optimization search.
Kudyshev
et al.311 integrated a c-AAE
with an optimization algorithm to search for the optimal thermal emitter
design with enhanced efficiency. The thermal emitter comprises the
titanium nitride (TiN) back reflector, a silicon nitride (Si3N4) spacer, and a TiN plasmonic antenna in the top layer
(see Figure 42a).
The top antenna image is appended with the spacer thickness and periodicity
of the array to form the input to c-AAE. The primary objective of
the optimization is to find the optimal shape/topology of the top
antenna, the array periodicity, and the spacer thickness, which collectively
result in high emissivity within the working band range of 0.5–1.7
μm. The c-AAE network contains an encoder (E), a decoder/generator (G), and a discriminator
(D), as shown in Figure 42b. The E network compresses
the input design (x) to the 17-dimensional compressed
space, and the coupled G network decompresses the
compressed space back to the original design space. The E and G networks are trained by minimizing the reconstruction
loss between input (x) and generated (x̃) designs. Following training, the G network can
generate new designs given the input compressed space vector z̃ = E(x), which
is a 15-dimensional coordinate vector appended with two conditional
labels l (unit cell size and spacer thickness). To
efficiently evaluate the performance of the generated designs, the
G network is further combined with a conditional Visual Geometry Groupnet
(c-VGGnet) network to estimate the efficiency of the designs based
on the input binary image of the antenna. This avoids the need for
time-consuming full-wave simulations (see Figure 42c). The loss evolution during the training
of the c-VGGnet is displayed in Figure 42d, and the decreasing regression loss indicates
that the c-VGGnet accurately retrieves the efficiency values based
on the input design image. Figure 42e illustrates the comparison between the predicted
efficiency by c-VGGnet and the true values, achieving a sufficiently
high value of r2 = 0.87.

(a) The thermal emitter
design. (b) Training workflow of the c-AAE
network. (c) The trained G network is coupled with
a c-VGGnet for rapid efficiency estimation. (d) Evolution of the training
(blue line) and validation (red line) losses of the c-VGGnet for efficiency
prediction. (e) The regression results performed by c-VGGnet on the
testing data set. White line shows the regression line, and the colormap
shows the number of designs tested. (f) Scheme of the c-AAE based
global optimization algorithm. (g) Spectral emissivity of the best
designs generated by global optimization (red) and randomly generated
(blue). Reproduced with permission from ref (311). Copyright 2021 De Gruyter.
During the optimization process (see Figure 42f), a differential
evolution (DE) optimizer
explores the compressed design space and proposes candidate solutions
to the c-AAE generator. The G network then reconstructs
the design, and the efficiency of the thermal emitter is evaluated
using the c-VGGnet, providing feedback to the optimizer. Based on
this feedback, the optimizer updates its searching parameters for
the subsequent optimization step. This iterative process continues
until the optimal design, hidden within the compressed design space,
is identified. The c-AAE network is then employed to retrieve the
corresponding unit cell configuration of the optimal design. It is
worth highlighting that the proposed approach utilizes a global optimizer
as a black box, offering flexibility to couple the developed c-AAE-based
framework with other optimization techniques. Figure 42g illustrates the efficacy of this approach,
where the red curve represents the absorption spectra of the best
design proposed using the c-AAE-based optimization method, demonstrating
notably high absorption within the working range.
Apart from
TPV systems, thermal emitters find more practical applications
when their emissivity wavelength can be tuned to desired regimes.
For instance, carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless, and tasteless
gas, but it is extremely poisonous to humans being. Therefore, the
development of a low-cost method for CO detection is of paramount
importance. To address this, Granier et al.312 have successfully employed the genetic algorithm for designing an
aperiodic multilayer structure with alternating layers of silicon
and silica on top of a semi-infinite tungsten substrate. The optimized
structure exhibits a narrowband and highly directional emittance at
the frequency λ = 4.7 μm, which corresponds to one of
the molecular resonances of CO. By heating the designed structure,
light is emitted at the resonant frequency of CO (λ = 4.7 μm).
Subsequently, one can use a detector to search for dips in the intensity
of the 4.7 μm light through absorption spectroscopy. Such dips
signify an increase in the concentration of CO in the surrounding
environment, facilitating effective and precise CO detection.
It should be
noted that the optimization of the thermal emitter is only one aspect
of the entire thermophotovoltaic device. Another crucial component
that significantly influences the energy harvesting performance of
the entire system is the thermal absorber. The thermal absorber is
responsible for converting incident solar radiation into thermal energy.
Its efficiency plays a vital role in the overall energy conversion
process. For effective energy harvesting, the thermal absorber needs
to efficiently absorb radiation in the visible and near-infrared (NIR)
range while minimizing emission in the infrared (IR) regime. Achieving
this spectral selectivity often involves modifying the geometrical
parameters of nanostructures within the absorber. Among the various
proposed selective absorbers, those based on multilayer structures
have gained significant interest313,314 because the
number of its potential structure candidates are enormous to be explored
with machine learning method.
Zhou et al.315 have trained the artificial neural network to accelerate
the optimization process of the genetic algorithm searching for an
ultrawideband perfect absorber (UWPAs) from 8 to 14 μm, as shown
in Figure 43a. The
unit cell is a five-layer absorber structure consisting of alternating
thin layers of Ti and GaAs. To improve the convergence rate and prediction
accuracy, the parameters vector and the output absorbance vector are
normalized by the Min-Max scaling method. Note that the neural network
is a surrogate model to predict spectral absorbance given the vector
structure parameters. Input geometrical parameters are the vertical
thickness and the width of each GaAs layer as well as the ratios of
these dimension quantities. Thanks to the neural network, it takes
only 573 s to generate 1.2 × 105 configurations. Compared
with the conventional electromagnetic simulation software (FDTD Solutions),
the computational cost is reduced by 4 orders of magnitude. At normal
incidence, the optimal structure shows four resonant peaks in the
8–14 μm, and the mean absolute errors (MAEs) between
actual and predicted absorbance is only 5.8 × 10–3. Besides, the average absorptance can be maintained to 1 within
the incident angle θ = ±45° and above 0.8 within the
incident angle θ = ±70°. Note that other metamaterial
absorbers cannot keep such a high absorbance under a large incident
angle. The absorbance performance has also been investigated, and
the mechanism turns out to be the strong magnetic field enhancement
generated between different layers at different incident wavelengths.

(a)
Thermal absorber design based on trained neural network to
accelerating the Genetic Algorithm optimization process. (b) Optimization
of thermal absorber by Genetic Algorithm. Reproduced with permission
from ref (316). Copyright
2014 Elsevier.
An artificial solar selective absorber is designed
to efficiently
absorb sunlight while minimizing thermal emission. As a result, the
temperature of the absorber rises during its operation. To ensure
optimal performance at elevated temperatures, tungsten emerges as
a promising candidate material due to its high melting point. Moreover,
tungsten is a refractory metal with high absorption losses in the
visible and near-infrared (NIR) spectral range, making it an excellent
choice for enhancing sunlight absorption. Based on the tungsten–silica
(W-SiO2) cermet as the intermediate layer, Sakurai et al.316 optimized a multilayer selective thermal absorber
by tuning each layer’s thickness and tungsten volume fraction
within the cermet layer through the genetic algorithm, as shown in Figure 43b. They generate
20 initial populations of the absorber structures with various code
strings. Each generated individual is a code string of chromosome
and is assigned the parameters of layer thickness and the metal volution
fractions as the genetic information. During the optimization process,
a pair of elite structures are selected for mating. For the crossover
and mutation operations, part of the code strings is randomly changed
to produce new offspring. After evaluating the Figure of Merit, the
individual with high absorbance is kept as the next generation while
the poor one is discarded. Finally, pick out the best structure at
the termination stage. Their optimal structures with different layer
numbers all achieve solar absorbance of nearly 1, even under the illumination
of a quite low thermal emittance. Therefore, applying the genetic
algorithm directly can solve the optimization problem in designing
thermal absorber.
In another example, Wang et al.317 also
selected tungsten comprising the intermediate layers of a multilayer
thermal absorber. They utilized Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm
to optimize the thicknesses of each layer and experimentally fabricated
the optimal sample by sputtering and chemical vapor deposition techniques
on the wafer scale. The spectral absorbance is validated to be larger
than 0.95 by a Fourier Transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR), under
a low solar emittance that less than 0.1 in the mid-infrared. The
layer composition from top to bottom is: SiO2–Si3N4–W–SiO2–W. They
also selected tungsten as one of the layer materials due to its high
melting point that can make the entire absorber to work at high temperature.
This has been verified by thermal cycling test that the developed
multilayer absorber is thermally stable at 400 °C for up to 72
h heating in air. A Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm is proposed
by Wang et al.318 to optimize the Tamm
emitters. They have achieved a high Q-factor of 508 and an emissivity
peak 0.92 at 4.255 μm, far surpassing the previous results.
Recently, Seo et al.319 utilized a machine
learning surrogate model to optimize the grating structure for a broadband
thermal absorber. The researchers trained a DNN to replace the computationally
intensive rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA) method in computational
electrodynamics. By employing the DNN as a surrogate model, they accelerated
the particle swarm optimization algorithm during design process. For
the absorbing material, they chose Cr due to its strong intrinsic
absorption, supporting plasmonic resonance in the visible spectrum.320 The dimensional parameters (i.e., period Λ,
grating width w, grating thickness dg, thickness of topmost SiO2 layer duf, and thickness of bottom SiO2 film dbf) of the grating structure are used as input
layer of the DNN model, as shown in Figure 44a. To train the DNN model, they adopted
the active learning method. They started with an initial data set
of 300 samples and iteratively added 50–100 more samples to
the data set after each validation step until the RMSE was reduced
to a certain criterion value. Ultimately, the DNN model achieved an
impressive RMSE of only 0.003 with a total of 1566 training samples.
The optimized solar absorber design achieved near-unity spectral absorptance
over a wide wavelength range from 400 to 1000 nm (see Figure 44b). The time-saving benefit
of using the DNN model was significant compared to the original RCWA
simulation, with the DNN model requiring less than 0.1 s for estimation
instead of approximately 20 min for RCWA. This substantial reduction
in computation time greatly expedited the entire optimization algorithm,
enabling about 500 million estimations. To validate the optimal design,
the researchers experimentally fabricated a simplified structure by
changing the square hole in the Cr grating to a circular hole. This
simplification was acceptable because the absorptance spectra of the
two structures were nearly identical (see Figure 44c,d), and the measured solar absorptance
of the fabricated optimal design was 0.916.

Cr based grating solar absorber. (b) Absorption
spectra with optimum denoted as red dotted. (c) Original square hole
and simplified circular hole grating structure. (d) Absorption spectra
calculated by RCWA method for fishnet grating structure (blue with

To maximize the evaluation factor of the NFRHT,
Zhang et al.321 employed an adaptive hybrid
Bayesian optimization
algorithm to devise optimal aperiodic multilayer configurations for
both emitter and receiver components. Remarkably, the algorithm achieved
a significantly elevated evaluation factor of 3.98 × 105 W/m2 by examining a mere 2.6% of the samples encompassing
a vast pool of 1.0 × 108 W/m2 candidate
structures drawn from the database. By incorporating the nonvolatile
phase-changing material Ge2Sb2Te5 (GST) for designing the wavelength-selective emitter (Au-GST-Au
configuration), Song et al.322 hybridized
Bayesian optimization with the transfer matrix method, thereby orchestrating
high emissivity within the 5–8 μm wavebands and concomitant
low emissivity within the 3–5 μm and 8–14 μm
regimes. Impressively, this algorithm discerned the optimal structure
by evaluating less than 0.027% of the total candidates, with remarkable
peak emissivity of 0.95 at a wavelength of 5–78 μm.
So far, we have discussed
the separate optimization of thermal emitter or absorber of a TPV
system using machine learning approaches. For a near-field thermophotovoltaic
(NF-TPV), the solar absorber and the thermal emitter are included
in the intermediate structure denoted as the solar transfer section.
Another important subsection of the NF-TPV system is the conversion
section, which is comprised of the thermal emitter and a PV cell.
Therefore, the efficiency of the entire STPV system is calculated
by the multiplication of solar-to-absorber efficiency at the intermediate
layer, and the emitter-to-PV cell efficiency (i.e., PCE). Due to the
tradeoff between solar transfer efficiency and PCE through the emitter
temperature TH at the intermediate structure,
it is difficult to design the PV cell structure to achieve high efficiency
for the entire STPV system. To maximize the efficiency of the entire
STPV system, Song et al.323 have combined
artificial neural network with genetic algorithm to produce optimal
the PV cell design parameters at different emitter temperature TH ranging from 1200 to 2000 K (see Figure 45).
In particular, the PV cell is a multijunction structure, composed
of multiple subcells that are interconnected in series. Each sublayer
is made of GaxIn(1–x)AsySb(1–y) and the combination of x and y determines the bandgap energy. The design variables include
the thickness and bandgap energy of each sublayer, as well as the
emitter temperature TH. The optimal PV
cell can yield the system efficiency of above 25% at 1200 K and higher
than 42% at 2000 K.

Schematic illustration of the multijunction-based
near-field solar
thermophotovoltaic system.
Another application
of selective thermal radiation is radiative cooling, a phenomenon
in which objects cool down by radiating electromagnetic waves. The
Earth’s atmosphere is transparent in the infrared (IR) wavelength
range of 8–13 μm, namely the heat radiation from the
Earth’s surface will go directly to out-space, which acts as
an extensive thermal reservoir because of its low temperature (3 K).
This characteristic facilitates a passive cooling mechanism for terrestrial
bodies at ambient temperature, dissipating heat through radiative
emission. Considering all heat exchange processes (see Figure 46), the net cooling power Pnet of a radiative cooler can be expressed as
where Pr = 2π
∫π/20 sinθ cosθ dθ ∫∞0LBB (Tr,λ) er (λ,θ) dλ is the radiative power emitted
by the radiator, and Pa = 2π ∫π/20 sinθ
cosθ dθ ∫∞0LBB (Tr,λ) er (λ,θ) ea (λ,θ) dλ is the amount of
absorbed incident radiation from atmosphere. The emissivity of the
radiator er (λ,θ) can be defined
by its absorptivity according to the Kirchhoff’s law. The emissivity
of the atmosphere is given by ea (λ,θ)
= 1 – t(λ)1/cosθ, where t(λ) is the atmospheric transmittance in the zenith
direction.324Tr and Ta represent the temperature of
the radiator and ambient temperature, respectively. Pnonrad stands for the nonradiative (i.e., conductive and
convective) heat absorbed by the radiator from the surrounding media. Psolar denotes the absorbed solar power by the
radiator during the daytime. To overcome the adverse effects of solar
radiation, recent advancements in cooling devices have incorporated
features that enable them to function as simultaneous solar reflectors
and IR radiators. These coolers effectively reflect 97% of the incident
solar radiation while still radiating significant IR emission within
the 8–13 μm wavelength range,325 enabling efficient radiative cooling.

cooler. The

To maximize the cooling
rate, a radiative-cooling device must exhibit maximal emissivity within
the spectral range of 8–13 μm. Moreover, for an emitter
designed for daytime cooling, its absorptivity in the visible and
near-infrared range should be minimized to reduce heating from incident
solar radiation. Initially, engineered radiative coolers relied on
simple bulk materials, such as pigmented paints.326 Recent years have witnessed the extension to nanostructured
materials like resonant SiC and SiO2 nanoparticles,327 and the hybrid structure comprising a lossy
photonic crystal reinforced by a thin-film reflector.196 Further development in radiative cooling technology
involved the incorporation of layered systems,197 metasurfaces,328 photonic crystals,329 and hierarchically porous polymer coatings.330
The grating structure has also been applied
to radiative cooling,
in which spontaneous thermal emission from an object exceeds the heat
influx, such as absorption of solar irradiance, nonradiative heat
transfer via conduction and convection.197,331 As shown in Figure 47a,b, Seo et al.332 presented an optimized
complex grating structure using the genetic algorithm, accelerated
through a well-trained ANN. For the grating elements in the hexagonal
array forming the unit cell, SiO2 and Al2O3 were selected due to their high absorption capability and
advantages in systematic lifespan.333 The
incorporation of the surrogate model significantly reduced the computational
time, enabling the prediction of the radiation power of a specific
grating structure in just several milliseconds, compared to one hour
in traditional simulations. The optimal structure resulted in a daytime
radiative cooling power of 89.2 W/m2, associated with a
cooling temperature of 10.1 °C below the ambient temperature
(see Figure 47c,d).
Through finite-difference-time-domain (FDTD) simulations, the researchers
revealed that the electric field was strongly confined around the
SiO2 grating element, while the magnetic field was highly
concentrated inside the SiO2 grating element (see Figure 47e,f). These two
effects resemble the localized surface phonon–polariton and
cavity resonance, which suppress polar-angular sensitivity. The optimal
structure demonstrated promising potential for cold energy harvesting
in plain areas and rooftops of buildings.

complex grating structure from top view. (b)

Recently, Song et al.334 have undertaken
the design of an optimal surface structure featuring Polydimethylsiloxane
(PDMS) gratings through the amalgamation of a genetic algorithm, facilitated
by an artificial neural network. The culmination of their efforts
has led to the creation of a PDMS grating structure that exhibits
an outstandingly elevated emissivity value achieving 0.99. Notably,
PDMS silicone elastomer stands endowed with promising attributes for
radiative cooling, such as compatible optical properties, ease of
fabrication, and economic affordability.335,336 Nevertheless, their work could be further improved by setting the
radiative cooling power as the objective function rather than the
emissivity to prove the feasibility of PDMS utilized in radiative
cooling. In addition, combining Bayesian optimization with RCWA method
is another efficient approach to achieve radiative cooling, and the
optimal structure can be obtained by calculating only less than 1%
of the total candidate hybrid grading and multilayer structures.337 Besides, Li et al.338 have trained machine learning methodology in concert with the genetic
algorithm to realize daytime radiative cooling. This pioneering undertaking
leveraged a five-layer film structure, whereby the prediction accuracy
of the adeptly trained surrogate model demonstrates an average error
of approximately 0.56%. Moreover, the computational efficiency has
been significantly augmented by the incorporation of the machine learning
model, rendering it 67-fold swifter compared to conventional methodologies
such as the transfer matrix method. The optimal device configuration
demonstrated a noteworthy reduction in ambient temperature by 9.08
°C under steady-state conditions.
Applying the PSO algorithm
directly is another effective approach
to optimize the structural parameters and materials of grating selective
structures, as demonstrated by Zhang et al.339 The design variables include the different materials Mi, the thickness parameters hi, li, and wi, and
the period of the grating selective structure expressed as Λi = li + wi (see Figure 48a). Silver is chosen
as the substrate due to its higher reflectivity in the visible and
near-infrared wavelengths. The net radiative cooling power Pnet is expressed as Pnet = Prad – Psun – Patm – Pnonradiative, where Prad is emissivity power of radiator surface, Psun is absorbed sun power, Patm is the absorbing power of atmospheric thermal radiation, and Pnonradiative are power absorbed by conduction
and convection. In the PSO algorithm (see Figure 48b), each particle represents a solution
with an array of design parameters, and its surface radiation property
is evaluated using the objective function based on Rigorous Coupled-Wave
Analysis (RCWA). The objective function is defined as the difference
between the ideal absorptivity and actual absorptivity in the 0.3–13
μm band, which should be minimized during the optimization process.
Each generation of particles has two optimal solutions: a global optimal
solution found so far and a local optimal solution at that generation.
By comparing these two optimal solutions, the position vector and
velocity vector of each particle are adjusted iteratively. The optimal
structure has achieved a cooling power 72.42 W/m2 during
the day and 121.47 W/m2 at night, when the emitter surface
temperature is equal to the outdoor ambient temperature (see Figure 48c). Its cooling
performance is better than 80% of the flat panel radiator. In addition,
Guo et al.340 designed radiative coolers
using Bayesian optimization and evaluated only less than 1% of the
total candidate structures, as shown in Figure 49. The structure model consisted of polydimethylsiloxane
(PDMS) and five alternating layers of TiO2 and silver.
Bayesian optimization effectively determined the optimal combination
of thickness for each layer.

Compared to previous studies that only geometrical
parameters are
cosidered, the design space can be significantly expanded by incorporating
relevant material properties. Sullivan et al.341 employed a deep neural network as a surrogate model to
explore a library of materials and discover optimal design parameters
for micropyramid structures used in radiative cooling applications.
The output layer of the neural network comprised two neurons to predict
the reflectivity (R) and transmissivity (T), from which the emissivity (ε) can be calculated
as ε = 1 – T – R. The geometry of the micropyramids in Figure 50a, involves three key parameters: the triangle
base span (xspan), height (zspan), and substrate thickness (tsub). In contrast to previous approaches that solely used geometrical
parameters as input, the authors enhanced the neural network input
by incorporating the injection wavelength (λ) and material data
appended to the geometrical parameters. Each wavelength points in
the FDTD simulation had corresponding optical properties linking the
output and material data. Therefore, a single wavelength point was
included as an additional network input. Furthermore, each wavelength
point was associated with refractive index values (n) and extinction coefficients (k), which are related
through the real and imaginary parts of permittivity (εreal and εim). The integration of these correlated
parameters strengthened the connection between input and output, leading
to a higher prediction accuracy (see Figure 50b). The MAE for training and validation
sets are reported as 0.0034 and 0.0035, respectively, and the MSE
for training and validation sets are 0.0034 and 1.53 × 10–4, respectively. The surrogate model can emulate the
FDTD results of over one million distinct combinations in less than
a minute, which is an 8 orders of magnitude improvement. Figure 50c illustrates the
materials and geometries identified by the search process that optimized
the cooling thermal balance at three different surface temperatures:
300 K, 500 K, and 1000 K. The comprehensive incorporation of material
properties and geometrical parameters in the surrogate model enabled
precise predictions, opening new avenues for efficient materials design
and optimization in radiative cooling applications.
