When algorithms are used to learn complex relationships between dependent and independent variables, the resultant model may become difficult to interpret. Such uninterpretable models are said to be “black box”. Today, there are ways of understanding how important a variable or set of variables is to the model. The ease of extraction and interpretation of importance measures can vary by algorithm, and with the software implementation of the algorithm being used. Broadly speaking, variable-importance measures can be dichotomized into measures that are specific to the ML algorithm itself and (2) measures that could be used with any ML algorithm (called model-agnostic methods)[70]. In the latter case, an examination of model performance when including and removing variable(s) may shed light on the relative importance of those variable(s), although for very large data sets and/or computationally demanding algorithms this may burden computing resources.
Variable importance – however it is measured – is not a panacea. It has been well-recognized within ML that an algorithm may find multiple optimal ‘solutions’ in terms of performance, sometimes with completely different sets of predictor variables (e.g., [71]). In addition, although statistical concerns such as multicollinearity in generalized linear models are well-known, the effects of these concerns (and others, such as predictors with different scales of measurement [72]) on ML are usually not easy to disentangle [57, 58]. Moreover, ranking of variable-importance lists can be unstable and may require some form of aggregation in order to improve performance [71, 73].
On the other hand, contemporary approaches to measuring variable importance for ML models may offer distinct benefits in the context of biomedical research. Some variable importance measures, called local measures, are computed for a single participant, and thus provide a sample-specific measure of variable importance. Such measures could reveal, for example, that while gene A is not used in the prediction of a disease for patient B, gene C is used in the prediction of a disease for patient D. One intuitive approach to local interpretability is the use of counter-factual explanations (CFE): by calculating, for a given sample, the minimal change in input(s) required to get the maximal change in model output, an analyst can begin to understand what input(s) most influenced the model’s original output [74]. Readers interested in model-agnostic methods, including local measures like CFE, can find a helpful overview in Chapters 8 and 9 of Molnar’s Interpretable Machine Learning textbook. Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) is another approach that has been used to interpret models both at the population and individual levels, which has significance for future endeavours in precision medicine [75].
ML methods can be particularly helpful when there exist many complex non-linear interactions within the data. Although interactions can be modelled explicitly during statistical inference, some ML methods can potentially learn them automatically from the data. Neural networks are capable of learning interactions automatically, but depending on the complexity of the network, interpretations may be embedded in highly dimensional representations that may be virtually impossible to interpret. The neural interaction transparency (NIT) framework seeks to alleviate this issue by enforcing sparsity using a strategy whereby interactions learned in the initial hidden layers of the network are kept separate throughout the remaining hidden layers [76]. For some problems, including interactions could improve the model performance. However, increased fit complexity may come at the cost of decreased model interpretability, or worse, at risk of overfitting noise instead of signal. It should not be assumed that ML will necessarily solve real-world problems that traditional inferential statistics cannot. Supervised learning algorithms can discover non-linear patterns that may yield more predictive power than linear models. Similarly, unsupervised learning algorithms can identify subgroups within unlabeled data, even when the definitions of these sub-groups are defined by complex rules.
ML algorithms can model irregular data that are not structured as a matrix or table. They can also learn from, and integrate, multiple types of data simultaneously, including matrix, image, text, audio, video, and graph.
In addition to combining multiple data inputs within a single model, some ML algorithms can also learn multiple outputs simultaneously, allowing the prediction of one output to benefit from the prediction of the others [77]. For example, MTL methods can produce a single model that predicts both disease risk and medication response. MTL is increasingly being used in biomedical research [78–83]. Compared with single-output learning, MTL can produce different types and structures of outputs with complex interactions (e.g., an entirely personalized treatment plan).
Although sample-size requirements vary depending on the specific task and research domain, modern ML methods generally require large sample sizes. Inadequate sample sizes can further exacerbate the other risks and challenges associated with ML studies. It is very hard to say how many samples is large enough, as this depends on many factors. Some methods may work well for applications with 100s-1,000s of samples, while others may require 10,000s-100,000s of samples. We advise analysts to rigorously evaluate their models to assess their robustness and conduct sensitivity studies with respect to the amount of data used to train the models. Although sample size is very difficult to specify in advance, learning curve analyses can indicate if adding additional samples would likely improve performance by mapping the convergence point of validation performance and training performance as the number of training examples increases [61, 84]. Generative models, such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) or generative adversarial networks (GANs), can allow investigators to augment small training data sets with synthetic data by generating values within the range from which real data were derived. As a result, synthetic data closely resemble real data while not being merely duplicates of it, which can be useful when collecting new data may be prohibitively expensive or infeasible.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns a rule that fits the training data but does not generalize well to new unseen data [1]. Data with many more features than samples and/or considerable noise are especially prone to overfitting. Excessive optimization of ML models can also result in an overfit model. Importantly, overfitting may go undetected when test sets are omitted or not used properly. As reviewed by Barnett et al., such problems have likely led to overestimates of the ability of ML models to classify disease based on genomic data [85]. One approach to address overfitting is a technique called “early stopping”, which involves monitoring the model performance on both the training and validation sets, and halting the training process once the model’s performance on the validation set begins to deteriorate. Another approach to address overfitting is for modelling to be done as part of a large, multi-center study, where patients from one center comprise the training and validation sets, while patients from another center comprise an external and fully independent test set. However, the direct sharing of biomedical data from multiple studies or study centers is not always possible due to data protection and privacy regulations, in which case federated learning can allow multiple sites to collaboratively train a ML model by leveraging a decentralized approach in which only the model parameters are learned and updated via encrypted sharing [86, 87].
Studies with many more variables (p) than samples (n) may suffer from the “curse of dimensionality” or the n ≪ p problem [88], whereby a model can be prone to overfit due to the many possibilities of feature sets that can be included in such a model [88]. Dimensionality reduction through feature selection [89–91], feature extraction, or feature engineering can help mitigate the challenges associated with the curse of dimensionality. However, if not used correctly, dimensionality reduction methods may themselves cause bias and overfitting, such as when both the training and validation datasets are incorrectly combined for dimensionality reduction (as opposed to the correct approach, which would be to perform dimensionality reduction only on the training data) [92–94]. Another approach is to incorporate methods of regularization which retain the ability of ML models to learn complex relationships when the number of parameters estimated is too limiting [95].
Leakage occurs when information from the test/validation data unintentionally “leaks into” model training. For example, performing feature selection on the entire data set prior to cross-validation (CV) can lead to overly optimistic performance estimates and overfitting. Instead, one should hold-out an external test set at the beginning of the analysis, then choose the best features and model parameters using an internal validation set. The external test set should only be used once to evaluate the performance of the final model, and should never inform feature reduction or model training. See Barnett et al. for examples of data leakage in genomic studies [85]. CV is a useful approach to find an optimal model configuration when the number of samples available is too limited to define independent training/validation/test sets. Common ways in which CV can be performed are as follows: 1) k-fold CV, in which samples included in a training dataset are randomly assigned to one of k possible non-overlapping but equally sized groups called folds. Samples in k-1 folds are selected for training in which feature selection is performed and model parameters are learned independent of the validation fold. The model is evaluated in the held-out fold, and the procedure is repeated until all folds are used for model evaluation. Model performance is then summarized over the validation folds. 2) Leave-one-site-out CV, is common in multi-center or multi-site designs. It is similar to k-fold CV, except that the grouping variable used to divided samples into training/validation sets are the study sites themselves. The process begins by using k-1 sites to select features and train a model which is then evaluated on the remaining held-out site. The process is repeated until each site is used as the validation sample. 3) Nested CV, describes an approach whereby CV can be used to tune multiple hyperparameters in a ML model without over-fitting. In nested CV, samples are randomly divided into one of k possible equally sized folds (commonly termed the “outer loop”). Samples in k-1 folds are chosen then further split into k possible folds (commonly termed “inner loop”). Different values for hyperparameters can be trained and evaluated using the inner loop. The process is repeated until all samples in the outer loop are used for model evaluation.
Some ML methods, especially “sophisticated” and well-performing ones like ensemble and deep learning models, can be difficult to interpret (although the development of “explainable” AI, (XAI), is an active area of research [70]). Unlike inferential statistics, many ML methods do not yield measures of associations, such as Odds Ratios (OR) or slope coefficients, that describe the nature of the relationship between independent and dependent variables. On the other hand, some ML methods, like rule-based methods can be interpreted more readily, though increased interpretability sometimes comes at the cost of decreased accuracy. Regardless of the ML method used, feature selection can aid interpretation by helping make the resultant model as parsimonious as possible, as demonstrated, for example, in a recent ML study of asthma that used recursive feature elimination (RFE) on RNA-sequencing data to reduce the number of features for classification models [14]. Specifically, using the RFE algorithm, the authors identified a panel of 90 genes whose expression profiles, interpreted through a logistic regression classifier, accurately predicted if a patient had asthma or not (positive and negative predictive values of 1.00 and 0.96, respectively; AUC of 0.994). This relatively small set of genes made it easier to study their relevance to the pathophysiology of asthma. In addition, one could first engineer new features using domain knowledge to make the selected features even more interpretable, for example, by transforming gene expression into gene ontologies prior to classification [96].
Datasets with categorical outcomes can be unbalanced, where one category is significantly overrepresented compared with the other(s) (e.g., because of low disease prevalence). This can cause problems for traditional ML classification methods, since they are generally designed for balanced classes [97]. In such scenarios, techniques like under-sampling, over-sampling (e.g., SMOTE), and bootstrapping can be used to balance the classes during model training [97]. Importantly, some commonly used performance measures, including accuracy and AUC of the ROC curve, can be misleading for imbalanced data [98, 99]. In these scenarios, it is recommended to use class-specific measures, especially the combination of precision, recall, and F-measure [98, 99].
Many common confounding factors present in psychiatric datasets can mislead an ML model. For instance, there may be systematic biases in age, sex, methods of data collection and data-acquisition sites that are associated with the predicted outcomes. When these confounds are not addressed explicitly, an ML model can “falsely” learn to predict certain outcomes simply by leveraging the confounds, potentially leading to biased models. If this happens, the model may not generalize to new real-world data. To address this, one could pre-process data by taking a stratified sample that balances out known confounders, or by “correcting” or “residualizing” the data with respect to the confounders [100]. Another option is to compare a model trained on the confounders alone with a model trained on the confounders and features of interest; the former can serve as a baseline against which to compare the latter [101]. Some ML methods, such as confounder filtering [102], “subtract out” the contribution of confounders directly during model building. Others, such as adversarial learning, force the model solution away from models that predict the confounding variables [103].
Alternatively, one might attempt to remove sources of heterogeneity from the data prior to an analysis. Some widely used techniques for identifying and correcting for these sources are principal component analysis (e.g., to detect sample-relatedness or population stratification using DNA sequence/genotyping data [104]) and surrogate variable analysis (e.g., to extract latent confounders from transcriptomic data [105]). Properly accounting for heterogeneity prior to training an ML model can help reduce its error and improve its generalizability. However, it is necessary to correct any biases using the training set only, and then apply the training-set corrections to the test set separately. Otherwise, information from the test set can leak into the training set. Because ML models leverage complex non-linear relationships, removing heterogeneity with such methods may not be successful if only linear sources of heterogeneity are removed.
Although the challenge of missing data is not unique to ML, it is nonetheless a problem that must be addressed during model training and deployment. Even if an ML model will train successfully in the presence of missing data, missing data can potentially limit model accuracy or even reduce model generalizability. Missing data are common occurrences in clinical data that can arise for a variety of reasons. For example, in the setting of a randomized controlled trial (RCT) there may be missing values for main outcome measures due a patient stopping treatment, whether because of non-compliance or because of an adverse event. When missing data is identified, it is important to consider the mechanism(s) behind the missing data (e.g., missing completely at random, missing not at random) and to handle the missing data appropriately. One approach to missing data involves replacing the data with predicted values, also known as imputed values. However, incorrectly imputing missing values can pollute the data with misinformation and thus impair the model further.
Personalized medicine has sparked enormous interest in ML. However, in order to successfully implement ML in clinical practice, one must overcome several technical challenges and ethical dilemmas posed by ML in healthcare. A complete list of all challenges and dilemmas is beyond the scope of this review, however, we highlight a few considerations below.
Data used for training ML models should ideally be large, diverse, high-quality, well-labelled, and accurately representative of the groups for which the models are intended to be used. However, even when “big data” are available, practical concerns may need to be addressed, such as heterogeneity. In healthcare decision-making, heterogeneity is commonplace, and could impair the generalizability of a model if the data encountered during deployment differ from the data used during training (e.g., because the data comes from a client cohort not represented in the training data, or because the methods used to collect the relevant input data differ between clinical and research settings). When collecting and processing data, adherence to field-standard protocols is an important step towards mitigating potential biases associated with heterogeneity.
The ethical and social ramifications of ML in healthcare are numerous and complex. Relevant ethical and social issues include, but are not limited to, concerns regarding informed consent, fairness [106], safety, transparency, patient privacy, just allocation of resources, quality assurance, trust, patient values, cyber-security, confidentiality, social justice, human rights, accountability, over-diagnosis/over-treatment, skill erosion, environmental sustainability, explainability/interpretability, liability, patient autonomy, patient choice, legal regulation, and information overload [107]. Given the number of issues that require consideration, those developing ML for healthcare settings may wish to consult ethical guidelines, or professional ethicists themselves, to help safeguard the public against the misuse of ML. In addition to upholding ethical principles, researchers may have to further comply with regulatory frameworks, with the U.S. Federal Drug Administration (FDA) issuing an action plan in 2021 describing an updated regulatory framework for AI technologies in healthcare that reinforced the importance of evaluating safety, effectiveness, and transparency of AI/ML [108].
Although prediction models can be extremely useful in clinical settings, they can have the unintended effect of continuing or worsening health care disparities. For example, this problem may occur when a model is developed in a group that is heavily weighted toward one ethnic, economic or another social group [109], such that the model might not be valid for other groups that had not been represented in the predictive modelling effort. This issue is especially acute for genomic data because most large samples have been collected from people with European-American ancestry. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that machine learning models are a “black box” that does not allow for easy interpretation of how these models make their decisions. To address these issues, modelling efforts should use data from multiple sources and assess accuracy, reliability, reproducibility and generalisability across countries, ethnicities and genders. Projects should adhere to the data principles of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) and assure the appropriate use and interpretation of data along with systematic efforts to reduce health care disparities by clarifying the relevance of algorithms to both genders and to minority groups. A useful resource is Fairlearn, an open-source, community project aimed at improving the fairness of AI systems (https://fairlearn.org/). The Fairlearn functions assess fairness metrics for racial, ethnic, gender, immigration status and other disparities.
The potential of ML to combine individual predictors/features with small marginal effects into a single predictive model, combined with the increasing availability of “big data”, has led to the increased adoption of ML in psychiatry. This has included studies on genetic association, gene expression, proteomics, metabolomics, methylation, neuroimaging, neuropsychological, clinical and other data sources [18, 20–23, 110, 111]. Like other areas of medicine [2, 10–14, 71], a broad spectrum of ML tasks have been pursued in psychiatry, such as predicting clinical diagnosis, clinical course, treatment response, and adverse events, as well as patient stratification and subgroup discovery.
As Figure 1 shows, we conceptualize trends in the use of ML in psychiatry along three dimensions: 1) from unimodal to multimodal data analysis (data richness); 2) from traditional statistical methods to modern ML tools, including deep learning (algorithmic complexity); and 3) from data-driven methods to those incorporating external domain-specific information (external information). The following sections review the use of ML in psychiatry and showcase emerging topics in the field.

Schematic illustration of trends in ML development relevant to psychiatric research.
We searched the literature and screened abstracts (Table S1) which identified 1,461 primary articles (published between January, 1977 and December, 2020) that in the title, abstract, or keywords reported using one or more supervised or unsupervised ML methods across 12 psychiatric phenotypes and four data modalities. 50.4% of the papers were published since 2015. Of the identified papers, 53.1% (n = 777) used a supervised method, 25.1% reported an unsupervised method, and the remaining using multiple or unspecified methods (Figure 2).

Most publications investigated schizophrenia or psychosis spectrum disorders (SCZ/PSD, 20.9%), followed closely by major depressive disorder (MDD, 15.6%). Other commonly studied phenotypes were substance use (SUDs, 11.0%), sleep (7.5%), and anxiety (4.9%) disorders (Figure 3). 20.1% of the studies addressed multiple psychiatric disorders.

Surprisingly, despite its relatively recent growth, studies applying ML to genomic data comprised a very small percentage of the ML in psychiatry literature (0.4%) (Figure 4). Although there are a multitude of advantages associated with ML compared to less-complex models such as generalized regression, as discussed in our section “Opportunities and Challenges of ML”, important considerations remain regarding data- or study-specific factors that may limit the effectiveness of ML. There are several situations in which the use of ML or DL has a distinct advantage over simpler models like generalized regression, but there are others in which they may not be as effective. ML should not be considered a guarantee of superior performance as evidenced by prominent examples in the literature of generalized regression models yielding similar or better performance relative to ML [112, 113]. In the context of biological psychiatry, there are examples in which generalized regression models have either outperformed ML, as in the case of predicting PTSD treatment response from clinical and demographic measures, or have shown comparable performance to ML, as in the case of gene expression-based diagnostic classifiers of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [114, 115]. The importance of evaluating the trade-off between model complexity and interpretability becomes increasingly evident in situations where ML performs similarly to generalized regression models. There are several unique benefits that could influence the decision to choose generalized regression over ML, such as the ability to update the model with continuously collected data, the interpretability of model coefficients, and easily assessing the significance of individual predictors. Nevertheless, ML has distinct advantages over generalized regression models when, for example, problems are far too complex to be abstracted into a regression model or there is a lack of domain knowledge that prevents interactions from being pre-specified. Furthermore, the ability of ML to be adapted to generative multi-task learning approaches poses unique advantages compared to non-ML models, such as the ability to augment small datasets with realistic synthetic data or designing adversarial tasks to combat the presence of confounding factors.
Interest is growing around the use of multiple data modalities to better understand psychiatric disease, since each of these modalities may provide complementary information about the disease being studied [116]. Recent applications include subgroup identification among patients with psychiatric conditions [117], dimensional analysis of psychopathology [118], and sub-group identification based on biomarkers and imaging [119–121]. Although promising, multi-modal analyses can be limited by the high dimensionality of the data. One way to address this limitation is to use lower dimensional feature aggregates for each modality. For example, genetic association data, in the form of polygenic scores, have been integrated with neuroimaging and cognitive data[122]. Another combined genome-wide association study (GWAS) and voxel-wise functional neuroimaging data [123]. This work suggests that combining data modalities can improve predictive accuracy. Another approach builds “base” models from the individual datasets, and aggregate these complementary base models into integrative ensembles [119, 120, 124].
Deep learning is increasingly being adopted in biomedical research [125], including psychiatry. These applications have included analyses of neuroimaging data [22, 35, 36], drug response [126], and genomic data [127]. One study [128] applied deep belief networks for the analysis of structural and functional brain-imaging data of patients with schizophrenia and healthy controls. This indicated that important physiological representations captured by other techniques (i.e., independent components analysis, or ICA) could be learned, and that the diagnostic classification could potentially be improved by further deepening the algorithm’s architecture. Deep learning is likely to play an important role in the future of psychiatric research, especially as larger and more complex data cohorts and XAI methods become more widely available.
Some ML applications may benefit from incorporating external information for tasks like feature engineering or model architecture design. Relevant external information includes linkage disequilibrium structure, biological pathways, Gene Ontology annotations, protein-protein interactions, and other biological systems-level data. Linkage information has been successfully integrated into conventional polygenic scores using a Bayesian approach to increase the explained variance by 5% for the prediction of schizophrenia [129]. Similarly, Linkage-disequilibrium-score regression has been used to distinguish confounding from polygenicity in psychiatric GWAS studies [130]. Another interesting application of external information integration is the combined analysis of multiple polygenic scores for the prediction of complex traits. This multi-polygenic score approach yielded more accurate predictions by leveraging the increased statistical power derived from multiple underlying GWASs [131, 132]. The design of clever ways to incorporate the constantly growing psychiatric knowledge into ML models is expected to yield even more accurate and informative models in the future.
Other ML approaches have incorporated biological pathway information in hierarchical procedures that build pathway-specific classifiers that are subsequently combined to yield biological systems-level predictors [133]. Such biologically informed ML was shown to outperform corresponding approaches that did not use this information when applied to transcriptome-wide expression and genome-wide DNA methylation data [133]. Another study used gene-set information to calculate gene-set polygenic risk scores, which in combination with genome-wide polygenic risk scores explained 8% more of the known genetic variance in ADHD compared to a genome wide only approach [85].
Some efforts have been made to formulate interpretable models for neuroscience applications. For example, Vu et al. proposed using the XAI framework [134], suggesting that ML models should be built on known neurobiological knowledge, and that the selected features should have simple and interpretable relationships. This approach favors models that are explainable even if their accuracy is lower than more obscure models. This approach, however, may bias models towards currently available knowledge, precluding novel discoveries. Vu et al. suggested that good models are defined as the ones that can be validated across different subjects and biological contexts [134]. Thus, future research should weigh the importance of interpretability vs. performance and novelty when choosing an ML method.
While state-of-the-art ML approaches are rapidly gaining attention in psychiatric research, ML has been widely applied in other areas of biomedicine, where it has shown impressive diagnostic and prognostic performance in fields like oncology and radiology [2, 10–14, 135–139]. Despite the studies exploring ML described above, the broader psychiatric research community has not yet fully embraced ML as a keystone to an effective and accountable research practice. Below, we consider some of the challenges and opportunities at the interface of psychiatry and ML.
Open-science initiatives, which aim to increase transparency at all stages of the scientific process, including data generation and result reporting, are being discussed in the psychiatric community [140]. Openly available data enables scientists to evaluate the reliability and reproducibility of ML-based models [141, 142]. Although the sharing of individual-level, personal health data is often restricted due to ethical and privacy concerns, methods of data de-identification can help build anonymized datasets and reference databases [143]. An example of a publicly available resource is the National Institute of Health (NIH) Database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (dbGaP), a large multi-modal repository of various phenotypes, which includes psychiatric disorders. Additionally, specialized consortia, such as the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (PGC), have collated large datasets that allow associated and external researchers to conduct independent research and replication studies [144].
As the volume of ML results increases, there should be an ongoing effort to catalog variations in the architecture and performance of published ML models to increase the visibility and accessibility of the field. An analogy is the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog, which manually curates results and summary statistics from published GWAS [145].
An essential requirement for reproducing the results of computational analyses, including those based on ML, is the public availability of the source code used in the study; this includes random-number seeds used during the analysis. Thus, along with data, researchers are recommended to publicly share their analysis code through services like GitHub [146] or open-source research platforms like Synapse [147]. Data Integration.
Studies using ML approaches in psychiatry use data derived from various modalities; however, as is currently the trend in scientific research, future studies will begin to put more emphasis on data integration [116]. While data integration may not necessarily increase the number of observations, integration across modality (e.g., multi-omics) will allow researchers to generate high-quality, well-characterized datasets that might improve model performance [148]. Among the largest datasets available for psychiatric phenotypes, the PGC has hundreds of thousands of individual samples across nine broad psychiatric phenotypes and integrated clinical and genomic data [144]. However, such retrospective integration is limited by standardization of methodology [149]. In response, prospective studies are similarly beginning to generate multi-modal data as part of the study design with the ultimate goal of integrated predictive modelling (e.g., CANBIND [150]). ML may prove useful in handling the scale and complexity of these data.
With increasing data availability and model complexity, the task of identifying the features that are most relevant to the process or phenotype of interest becomes more difficult [151]. In the context of ML, relevance can be defined in several ways, mainly pertaining to the contribution of each feature to the overall model. However, just because a feature is predictive of an outcome or relevant to a model does not mean the feature is physically related to the phenotype being studied. In other words, ML is no substitute for biological validation. Thus, studies relying on ML should, whenever appropriate and possible, accompany their findings with biological experiments that explore putative molecular mechanisms further. As models and data become more complex, experimentation will be a critical source of validated mechanistic knowledge.
Finally, while ML may offer robust methods to aid precision medicine, further integration of ML approaches will require an understanding of ML methods across the psychiatry community. Multidisciplinary collaborations will require educating the next generation of psychiatry professionals in ML [152]. Such training can include institutionally approved courses, educational workshops at recognized world-wide psychiatric conferences, and clinical training modules as part of continuous medical education. We hope that this review contributes to these education and training efforts.
The current landscape of ML models in psychiatric healthcare faces a major challenge with delivering reliable prognostic and diagnostic values at the individual level. Significant improvements in ML models have contributed to the general advancement of AI in psychiatry. This is particularly true for identifying broad trends and patterns in large patient cohorts, enabling AI to outperform human experts on some rapid and automated tasks in clinical settings [153, 154]. However, individual-level diagnostic and prognostic values produced by ML models can be unreliable due to various factors. These include biases present in the training data, disparities arising in data distributions between the training dataset and external datasets where the models are implemented, and constraints on model explainability, among other considerations. Given the possible impact of these factors on model performance, it is essential to ensure that standardized techniques are used to effectively measure the degree of ML model uncertainty. For example, individual-level diagnostic and prognostic values should always be presented with some indication of uncertainty or variance in estimation akin to confidence intervals. This level of disclosure will can increase transparency, trust, and consumer and clinician confidence when ML models are used as aids for clinical decision-making. While confidence intervals can be effectively estimated for predictions derived by linear regression, the assumptions inherent to linear models do not apply to ML models. As a result, methods such as Monte Carlo dropout [155], deep ensembles [156], and test time augmentation [157] have been developed to estimate the uncertainty of ML model predictions. In certain instances where predictions with low confidence are produced, it may be necessary to implement a manual requirement for models to abstain from making predictions [158]. As ML/DL tools are increasingly explored in clinical settings, it becomes essential for guidelines to emphasize the integration of uncertainty estimates, which in turn contributes to the ethical and safe use of models for diagnostic and prognostic purposes.
Additionally, the landscape of ML exploration in psychiatric healthcare will need to address the pragmatic hurdles associated with multiple coexisting diagnoses, fluctuations in clinical manifestations over time, and the presence of comorbid conditions which can impact of the accuracy of decision-making in personalized medicine. Thus, it is important that the training of ML models on large patient groups accounts for these complexities, interactions, and dynamics. As psychiatric conditions exist along a continuum of severity, ML models of these conditions must also shift away from artificial classification dichotomies. Instead, the ML models of the future should incorporate a variety of diagnostic indicators while taking into account comprehensive health records, environmental factors, presence of concurrent medical conditions (e.g., alcohol use disorder co-occurring with depressive disorders), and shared characteristics across a range of psychiatric conditions (e.g., similar clinical characteristics of eating disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, overlapping genetic and clinical characteristics of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder) to generate more realistic, natural, continuous estimates of impairment, treatment-response, etc. Increasing the quantity, quality, and seriality of patient data may help to meet the pragmatic requirements of ML-driven personalized medicine solutions that can effectively consider the overlapping and interconnected aspects of psychopathology when deriving diagnostic and prognostic estimates for individuals.
Concurrent with the development of this review, Tandon and Tandon recently stated: “It is, however, vital that an expert group of scientists and clinicians in psychiatry, neuroscience, machine learning, research methodology, neuroethics, and scientific publication convene to formulate a common set of guidelines for scientific reporting of ML studies in psychiatry.” [159]. We fully endorse this sentiment. The introduction of a cohesive ML consortium in psychiatry will improve advocacy for open science in the area and generate consensus for reporting guidelines which will ultimately improve the uptake of ML in psychiatry according to best practices. Responding to this need, we propose to form MLPsych, the Machine Learning consortium in Psychiatry, which will have the following initial objectives:
To serve as an ML interest group, and share methods, data, and novel discoveries made using ML for the mutual benefit of the consortium members and the field at large.
To host a clearinghouse of ML-friendly big data sets, such as the many transcriptomic datasets we generated and aggregated from the public domain and from consortium members [43, 50, 56, 115].
To generate and share synthetic datasets, allowing evaluation of feature selection algorithms, dataset characteristics, ML algorithms, and new methods.
To curate psychiatric ML reporting guidelines as needed (see Supplementary Table 1 for suggested Guidelines for REporting Machine Learning Investigations in Neuropsychiatry, or GREMLIN).
To identify a set of core ML experts who can be drawn upon to advise in the design of big-data projects.
To facilitate the entry of others into the field of ML through outreach, inclusion, and education.
To promote the fair, accountable, and transparent use of ML in accordance with emerging ethical and professional guidelines.
As we embark on these objectives in the coming years, we welcome the inclusion of all interested parties, either as contributors, consumers, or both.
In conclusion, with a foundation in the basics of ML, a sense of where the field has been in psychiatry, a set of guiding principles, and a formalized consortium, we hope that this review conveys that the future of ML applications in biological psychiatry holds great promise and potential.

Title: Harnessing the power of machine learning for crop improvement and sustainable production
Text:
Crop improvement and production domains encounter large amounts of expanding data with multi-layer complexity that forces researchers to use machine-learning approaches to establish predictive and informative models to understand the sophisticated mechanisms underlying these processes. All machine-learning approaches aim to fit models to target data; nevertheless, it should be noted that a wide range of specialized methods might initially appear confusing. The principal objective of this study is to offer researchers an explicit introduction to some of the essential machine-learning approaches and their applications, comprising the most modern and utilized methods that have gained widespread adoption in crop improvement or similar domains. This article explicitly explains how different machine-learning methods could be applied for given agricultural data, highlights newly emerging techniques for machine-learning users, and lays out technical strategies for agri/crop research practitioners and researchers.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, precision crop improvement, prediction model
Naturally, humans’ learning procedure is carefully or randomly monitoring surrounding events, grasping some experience and then predicting the next event, mainly occurring without human awareness. For instance, consider a human child who is learning how to talk. Basically, children do not know language learning techniques, procedures, or linguistics. Nevertheless, by listening to surrounding sounds, experimenting, and making mistakes, children gradually adjust their listening skills and simultaneously learn to talk and communicate in different situations. These procedures will continue until children feel confident enough to speak. Technically, they are learning how to talk by establishing a sound and an adequately accurate model of a whole set of procedures automatically and by testing the developed model again and again with surrounding voice data and improving it to build a more precise model. The term “machine learning” typically refers to the procedures of finding relevant groups within data or fitting prediction models to a target dataset. In essence, machine learning aims to mimic or resemble human capacity and the ability to identify patterns using computation approaches. Machine learning is especially handy when the dataset being analyzed is huge or sophisticated beyond human ability to analyze it or when we want to build an automated platform for analyzing a target dataset by considering it to be time-efficient and repeatable. Agricultural data often have these characteristics. Over the past few decades, agricultural databases have experienced remarkable growth in quantity and multi-layer complexity. Having a solid grasp of the methods being employed and some valuable tools for interpreting this wealth of data is becoming increasingly crucial. Although machine learning has been engaged in the crop domain for many years, its usage in agriculture and crop improvement has now become so widespread that it is used in almost every discipline. Only recently, though, has the field started to examine the various strategies more closely to determine which ones work best in certain situations or whether they are suitable at all. This review aims to offer compact, sufficient, and explicit information and details on how to use machine-learning techniques for agricultural and crop improvement researchers. We do not seek to provide a comprehensive analysis and investigate the literature on machine-learning applications for crop improvement problems nor to get into the specific mathematical details of different machine-learning techniques (Liakos et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2020). We focus on connecting specific machine-learning methods to various kinds of agricultural data. In addition, we will try to explain some best practices for approaching training and modeling improvement in real-world scenarios. The intrinsic intricacy of agricultural data poses opportunities and challenges for analytical methods in machine learning. We highlight common problems that undermine the validity of research and offer advice on how to overcome these challenges. The discussion of several machine-learning methods takes up most of this review, and we also provide explicit examples of how to use the strategy appropriately and understand the outcomes in each case. Traditional machine-learning techniques are included in the discussion as, in many situations; they continue to be the best options to apply. Our discussion covers techniques of deep learning, which shows satisfactory performance and is the best option for various machine-learning responsibilities. We also cover federated learning as a robust technique for having a machine-learning global crop improvement model to deal with future challenges such as climate change. We conclude by outlining the prospects for integrating machine learning into agricultural data analysis pipelines. When using machine learning in agriculture, there are two primary objectives. First, even though the collected data are sufficient or deficient, precise predictions should be made and used to direct further research endeavors. Since scientists are interested in understanding mechanisms, the other objective is to apply machine learning to enhance and increase the comprehension of crop improvement mechanisms, including several types of phenotypical, genotypical, biological, agronomic, and climatic mechanisms. We also summarize some of the limitations and applications of machine-learning approaches along with some data-related concerns for researchers in the crop improvement domain.
With emerging new technologies and approaches, large datasets are generated from different agricultural domains, particularly from the crop production domain. These vast datasets can easily feed into machine-learning approaches to help all beneficiaries optimize crop improvement systems. Even though machine-learning applications are extensive, their subcategories, mainly in crop quality (Elbasi et al., 2023; Attri et al., 2024), crop phenotyping (Gano et al., 2024), crop weed identification (Hu et al., 2021; Modi et al., 2023; Venkataraju et al., 2023), disease detection (Kulkarni and Shastri, 2024; Srinivas et al., 2024), crop recognition (Tian et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2023; Gafurov et al., 2023), crop-related microbiome improvements (Chang et al., 2017; Aguilar-Zambrano et al., 2023), and yield prediction (Van Klompenburg et al., 2020; Morales and Villalobos, 2023), were separated into crop development, production, and improvement, as shown in 
Figure 1
.

This schematic illustrates key applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning for crop development and improvement, including crop diseases, crop quality, crop species recognition, crop development, crop yield prediction, crop-related microbiome improvement, water management, soil management, etc. Farmers and researchers still encounter numerous obstacles due to employing traditional methods in the crop sector. Artificial intelligence and machine learning are used extensively to address these issues. Also, this figure shows possible data types and collection zones from crop fields to feed different machine-learning models to improve and develop different crops.
We discuss several fundamental ideas in machine learning and, whenever possible, present examples from agricultural literature to clarify these concepts.
A dataset consists of several instances, or data points, that are conceptualized as individual experimental observations. Several fixed features describe each data point. Phenotype, genotype (SNPs), product price, and climatic parameters are a few examples of these features. Whatever we aim to do with a machine-learning model is specified objectively by a machine-learning task. For instance, we could predict the rate of price fluctuation at a particular point in time for a specific agricultural product with an experiment examining the cost of the crop product over time. In this instance, the features “cost of crop product” and “time” could be referred to as input features. The conversion rate, which would represent the anticipated output of the target model at a specific moment, is the quantity we are interested in forecasting. Input and output features of a model can be as many as desired. Features could be either categorical (accepting just discrete values) or continuous (continuous numerical values are used). Technically, categorical features are usually binary in nature, meaning they can be 1 (true) or 0 (false).
Supervised machine learning describes how a model can be fitted to data or part of target data that distinct labels have received for which a ground truth attribute exists; this quality is often determined by experimentation, researchers, or data collectors. In contrast to knowledge derived from inference, ground truth is information verified via direct observation and measurement, thus known to be accurate or real (Kondermann, 2013). Among the examples are high-yield prediction (Panigrahi et al., 2023) and water quality prediction (Ahmed et al., 2019; Ghosh et al., 2023; Chatterjee et al., 2024) using supervised learning for crop improvement. Laboratory or experimental observations ultimately serve as the source of ground truth in both cases. Contrary to supervised learning, patterns in unlabeled data can be found using unsupervised-learning techniques (James et al., 2023). This approach does not require predetermined labels with ground truth information (Sindhu Meena and Suriya, 2020). For example, plant image data can be analyzed using an unsupervised machine-learning technique (Davis et al., 2020; Bah et al., 2023). Semi-supervised learning, in which a significant quantity of unlabeled data is paired with tiny quantities of labeled data, occasionally combines the two methodologies (Ouali et al., 2020; Ahfock and McLachlan, 2023); for example, weed distribution and density estimation (Liu et al., 2024). When obtaining tagged or labeled data is expensive, this can dramatically enhance performance. Another component of machine learning known as reinforcement learning (RL) teaches an agent how to behave and react in a given environment by having it carry out specific tasks and then watching the rewards or outcomes. This technique is already employed in different agricultural domains, such as crop yield prediction (Elavarasan and Vincent, 2020; Iniyan et al., 2023) and a completely autonomous precision agricultural aerial scouting technique (Zhang et al., 2020; Elango et al., 2024).
In machine learning, a task is referred to as a classification challenge when it requires allocating data points to a collection of discrete classes such as varieties emitting high or low methane, and a classifier is any algorithm that carries out this kind of classification (Sen et al., 2020), such as cassava disease detection and classification (Bian and Priyadarshi, 2024). Contrary to classification, regression models produce a collection of values that are continuous (Pardoe, 2020; Panigrahi et al., 2023), such as the prediction of yield before the harvest of very early potato cultivars by using a regression model (Piekutowska et al., 2021). Regression problems can frequently be reformulated as classification problems since continuous values can be discretized or thresholded (Greener et al., 2022). Typically based on some metric of data point similarity, in a target dataset, clustering algorithms are applied to predict and group similar data points (Ghosal et al., 2020). These techniques are unsupervised and do not necessitate labeling the instances inside a dataset. For example, according to images of soybean, clustering could predict seed weight (Duc et al., 2023).
When a classifier returns a discrete collection (set) of mutually exclusive values, such values are referred to as classes. These values are called labels when they do not have to be mutually exclusive. Typically, an encoding is used to represent classes and labels. One essential step in preparing data for machine-learning tasks is encoding categorical variables. It is essential to convert categorical data into a numerical format to make them compatible with machine-learning algorithms. Categorical data are not numerical values, such as categories or text. For example, a place variable with the values first, second and third or a color variable with the values; red, green, and blue is categorical data, which every value denotes a distinct category. There might be an inherent ordering or link between some categories. There is a natural ordering of values for the aforementioned place variable. There is a natural ordering of values for the aforementioned place variable. Due to the fact that the values can be ranked or ordered, this kind of categorical variable is known as an ordinal variable. There are several popular category encoding methods, each combining benefits and drawbacks such as label encoding, ordinal encoding, and one-hot encoding methods. One-hot encoding is one of these techniques, which is most frequently employed (Yu et al., 2022b). When there is no innate link or order among the categories, this encoding performs well with nominal categorical variables (Rodríguez et al., 2018). The distinctiveness of every category is maintained by one-hot encoding. It guarantees that no ordinal link between the categories is assumed by the method. Also, one-hot encoding eliminates the possibility of unintentionally adding biases based on the sequence of categories because each category is represented independently. But when working with categorical variables that have a large number of distinct categories, one-hot encoding can dramatically increase the dataset’s dimensionality. This may result in the curse of dimensionality and have an adverse effect on the performance of the model. Ordinal encoding is used when the categorical feature is ordinal. Every distinct category value in ordinal encoding is given an integer value. For example, in the color categorical data, red is 1, green is 2, and blue is 3. Maintaining the order is crucial in this method and encoding should so take the sequence into account. Equal intervals between categories are assumed by ordinal encoding, yet this may not always be the case in real-world situations (Dahouda and Joe, 2021). Unlike one-hot encoding, ordinal encoding does not increase the dimensionality of the dataset and It saves space and processing time by substituting integers for categorical variables. Label encoding assigns a unique integer value to each category in a categorical feature. This is an easy-to-use strategy that can be helpful when the categories’ order matters. However, because of the allocated integer values, it could create unintentional linkages between categories. For instance, label encoding could assign the values 0, 1, and 2 correspondingly if a categorical feature is small, medium, and large. This would suggest that “large” is twice as significant as “small”, which is probably incorrect. Important point is that the type of categorical variable and the issue those researchers are trying to solve will determine which encoding techniques should be used.
Machine-learning models never produce perfect results; they always deviate from the ground truth or the real world (Ho and Wookey, 2019). Cost or loss functions are the mathematical functions that compute this deviation or, more broadly, the degree of disagreement between the actual and ideal outputs (Uma et al., 2021). Mean squared error loss for regression problems is one example, and, for classification-related problems, binary cross entropy (Nar et al., 2019). A mean squared error loss function calculates the average squared difference between the anticipated value and ground truth. Binary cross entropy is a binary classification problem that must divide observations into one of two labels according to specific criteria [such as healthy leaf and infected leaf (Sarkar et al., 2023)].
In essence, models are mathematical functions that take a collection of imported features and return one or several features or values as an output. Models include adaptable and flexible parameters that can be adjusted throughout the training process to optimize the models’ performance, allowing them to learn from training data (Yu and Zhu, 2020). In a simple regression model, for instance, each feature has a particular parameter that is being multiplied by the value of the feature; these are then integrated and combined to provide a forecast. Hyperparameters are tunable values that are not changed during training and are thus not regarded as a model component. But this nonetheless affects the performance and training model. The learning rate, which regulates the pace at which the model’s parameters are changed during training, is a standard description of a hyperparameter. To simplify it, hyperparameters control a structure and training procedure of machine-learning models, and they might be the number of clusters in K-means clustering, the learning rate in a neural network, or the depth in a decision tree. Hyperparameters, in contrast to model parameters, need to be predefined and cannot be learned during training. A model’s ability to perform well or poorly can be determined by selecting the appropriate collection of hyperparameters. Therefore, choosing the set of hyperparameters that result in the best possible model performance is known as hyperparameter tuning. Depending on the type of model being trained, different sorts of hyperparameters may be employed including learning rate, number of epochs, batch size, number of hidden layers and units, regularization parameters, momentum, and activation function. Several tools are developed for model tuning and hyperparameter optimization such as Ray Tune (Shin et al., 2020), Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019), HyperOpt (Bergstra et al., 2015), and AWS Sage Maker (Das et al., 2020).
Models need to be trained, which is the process of automatically modifying model parameters to enhance performance before they can be used to generate predictions (Mathai et al., 2020) This means altering the parameters in a supervised learning setting to minimize the average value of the loss or cost function and improves model performance with a training dataset. Typically, a separate validation dataset tracks but does not alter the training process to detect any overfitting (Twomey and Smith, 1997). Even if a cost function does not run on ground truth outputs in unsupervised scenarios, it is nonetheless decreased. After training, the model can be evaluated using data not used during training (
Figure 2A
) (Eelbode et al., 2021). For a general overview of the training procedure and instructions on how to divide the target dataset into training set and testing set. 
Figure 2
 illustrates the principal notions for the training of models and displays a flowchart to aid in the whole procedure.

ML approaches for training. (A) Target data for machine learning should be split into training, validation, and testing sets. The training set is used to train the model directly. With the validation set, the training set is monitored. Test data are used to assess the performance of the model. The k-fold cross-validation approach is also used for validation. (B) Concept of underfitting and overfitting. (C) One-hot encoding is a process by which categorical variables are converted into a form that could be provided to ML algorithms to do a better job in prediction. (D) Numerical data can be represented in a way that machine-learning algorithms can understand using continuous encoding.
